answer: First, ensure clear communication; Then, follow traffic instructions; Next, report promptly at specified waypoints; After that, keep a safe distance from other vessels; Finally, avoid fishing gear and wrecks; Then, navigate with caution in narrow channels; Then, anchor in designated areas only; Then, do not drop anchor in the fairway. Do this correctly and reduced risk of accidents and environmental damage. Just be careful: anchoring in the fairway is prohibited.

question: Describe how to use VHF to report environmental hazards such as oil spills or floating debris.
gold_answer: For a significant hazard, use a SÉCURITÉ call on Ch 16 to alert nearby vessels, then contact the coastguard on a working channel with detailed information: type of pollutant or debris, exact position (lat/long + description), estimated size, drift direction and any source vessel observed. The coastguard will task the responsible authority (marine pollution response, harbour master) and log the report.
expected_points: then contact coastguard on working channel
answer: First, report pollution; Then, specify the type of pollution; Next, indicate the amount of pollution; After that, describe the movement of pollution; Finally, provide visibility conditions; Then, report traffic situation; Then, report weather conditions; Then, report sea conditions. Do this correctly and other vessels can navigate safely around the pollution. Just be careful: pollution may hinder navigation and pose risks to safety.

question: Explain how to phrase a report about a damaged navigation buoy in a constructive, factual manner.
gold_answer: Give the report as a SÉCURITÉ if the buoy is off-station or unlit at night, or as a routine call to the harbour authority in daylight for a minor damage. Content: identify the buoy (name, chart symbol, colour, top mark, MMSI if AtoN), state its state (off-station, unlit, damaged shape), position, time observed, and any hazard implication for shipping. Keep it neutral and factual; do not speculate on the cause.
expected_points: SÉCURITÉ if hazard to navigation (off-station or unlit at night)
routine call for minor damage in daylight
identify buoy (name, colour, top mark, chart)
answer: First, report the position of the damaged navigation buoy; Then, state whether the buoy is unlit or not; Next, describe the damage to the buoy; After that, indicate if the buoy is obstructing the channel. Do this correctly and other vessels will be informed of the navigational hazard and can take appropriate action. Just be careful: ensure the channel remains clear for safe navigation.

question: Describe how empathy and patience are important when dealing with inexperienced radio operators.
gold_answer: Novice operators may forget pro-words, take longer to compose messages, or use hesitant phrasing. A patient response — repeating information at a slower rate, using standard phrases, avoiding correction unless necessary — encourages them to keep using the radio and improve. Sarcasm or rudeness silences beginners and reduces overall safety on the channel because fewer people will call for help when they need it.
expected_points: repeat information at a slower rate
encourages continued use of the radio in emergencies
answer: First, repeat the last two digits of the call sign; Then, say 'I SPELL' before spelling out words; Next, read back the spelled-out word at normal pace. Do this correctly and clear communication of the intended message. Just be careful: do not say 'I SAY' when spelling.

question: Explain why shouting or using aggressive language on VHF can escalate tense situations.
gold_answer: Shouting overloads the audio and makes messages unreadable; aggressive language raises tension for both parties, encourages an equally aggressive reply, and creates a public example of poor conduct that others may copy. In an emergency it also slows the extraction of information by MRCC and may cause the transmitting vessel to be tuned out. Calm, structured phraseology is faster and more effective.
expected_points: aggression raises tension for both parties
answer: Because to ensure clear communication and maintain professionalism, and because to avoid escalating the situation further, and because VHF radio discipline is essential for effective communication, and because aggressive language or shouting should never be used over the radio.

question: Describe how inclusive and non-discriminatory language should be used on radio.
gold_answer: On a public channel, use neutral, professional language independent of gender, nationality, religion or background of the person addressed. Refer to vessels by name and to persons by role ("master", "skipper", "harbour master") rather than by assumed identity. Discriminatory or offensive remarks are prohibited by the ITU Radio Regulations and undermine the professional atmosphere required for safety communications.
expected_points: address vessels by name and persons by role
no assumptions on gender / nationality / background
discriminatory remarks are prohibited by ITU RR
answer: The word 'Over' indicates the speaker has finished their transmission and is awaiting a reply, and the word 'Out' signals the end of communication, indicating no response is expected.

question: Explain how good communication skills can improve cooperation with harbour staff and pilots.
gold_answer: Harbour staff and pilots respond well to skippers who identify their vessel promptly, give complete data (length, draught, ETA) on the first call, use standard phrases, and accept instructions with a readback. This cooperation reduces the number of exchanges required, speeds up berthing, and lowers the risk of misunderstanding during manoeuvres. Over time it builds a reputation of professionalism that helps at busy times.
expected_points: builds reputation and eases future visits
answer: First, use clear pronunciation; Then, speak at a moderate pace; Next, be patient and courteous. Do this correctly and improved clarity in communication.

question: Describe how to brief guests and novice crew about appropriate behaviour around the VHF set.
gold_answer: Before departure explain that VHF is a public safety channel: guests should not press the PTT or the DSC distress button, should keep their voices low near the cockpit speaker, and should ask before touching any control. Show them the on/off switch and Channel 16, and where the MAYDAY card is stored so they could use it in a genuine emergency. A calm two-minute brief covers the essentials.
expected_points: VHF is a public safety channel
guests should not press PTT or DSC distress
location of on/off and MAYDAY card
answer: First, brief guests and novice crew on proper VHF etiquette; Then, remind users to listen before transmitting; Next, inform users that emergency channels should only be used for emergencies; After that, advise users to monitor Channel 16 when operating on it; Finally, remind users to switch off their sets if they are not in use. Do this correctly and improved communication discipline among users. Just be careful: emergency channels should only be used in emergencies.

question: Explain how to manage radio use so that it does not disturb rest periods of crew and nearby vessels.
gold_answer: On extended passages agree a lower off-watch loudspeaker volume, route the DSC alarm to an on-watch cabin, use a headset when calling marinas or crew at unsocial hours, and avoid unnecessary calls late at night in busy anchorages where cockpit speakers carry across nearby vessels. Watchkeeping duty remains the same — Ch 16 and DSC must remain audible to the on-watch — but courtesy sets the extra volume level.
expected_points: route DSC alarm to on-watch cabin
watchkeeping still requires audible Ch 16 and DSC
answer: First, use the lowest power setting necessary for effective communication; Then, conduct routine discussions on VHF DSC Channel 70; Next, use designated channels for specific communications; After that, monitor Channel 13 when anchored; Finally, avoid unnecessary transmissions during specified hours; Then, cease transmissions if ordered by an authorized person or if harmful to safety. Do this correctly and reduced interference with other vessels' communications. Just be careful: failure to comply may result in penalties under the Radio Regulations.

question: Describe how to balance the need for urgent communication with respect for other users on a busy channel.
gold_answer: If your traffic is genuinely priority (safety of navigation, coordination with commercial traffic, a medical query) use the appropriate priority word (PAN PAN or SÉCURITÉ) and BREAK BREAK if you must interrupt. If it is routine, wait for a natural pause, keep the call short, and shift promptly to a working channel. Respect for other users is about correctly weighing your priority, not about staying silent.
expected_points: use priority word (PAN PAN or SÉCURITÉ) if genuinely urgent
BREAK BREAK to interrupt for priority traffic
routine traffic waits for a natural pause
keep calls short and shift channels
answer: First, monitor Channel 16; Then, use Channel 9 for initial contact; Next, switch to an appropriate working channel after initial contact. Do this correctly and effective communication is maintained while respecting channel usage protocols. Just be careful: avoid unnecessary chatter on emergency channels.

question: Explain how cultural differences might influence perceived politeness on the radio and how to adapt.
gold_answer: Formality, use of titles, tolerance of silence and directness of instructions vary between cultures — a UK skipper may find a French coast station more formal, a Dutch harbour master more direct, an Italian marina more expressive. Adapt by using neutral SMCP phrases, avoiding humour and idioms, saying "please" and "thank you", and matching the tone of the other station. Standard phraseology bridges cultural differences without requiring the operator to master each locally.
expected_points: formality and directness vary between cultures
match the tone of the other station
answer: Different cultures may have varying norms for politeness in communication, and it is important to be aware of these differences when using VHF radio.

question: Describe how to handle a misunderstanding on the radio without causing conflict.
gold_answer: If a message is misunderstood, request "SAY AGAIN" with the specific part, or offer "I SAY AGAIN" and restate your own information more slowly. Confirm agreement with a readback. Do not blame the other party publicly — misunderstandings are usually caused by noise, language or unfamiliar terms rather than incompetence. A neutral, factual approach preserves the working relationship for the rest of the passage.
expected_points: use SAY AGAIN for their message
use I SAY AGAIN for your own
answer: First, repeat the last transmission; Then, ask for their name and what they said; Next, say 'I misunderstood ...'; After that, state clearly what you heard; Finally, say 'What I understood is ...' and wait for confirmation; Then, say 'Is this correct?' and wait for an answer; Then, say 'Let me confirm: ...' followed by the corrected version; Then, say 'Thank you, I understood.' Do this correctly and both parties have a clear understanding of the communication. Just be careful: do not say 'I didn't hear you' or 'I can't repeat that' as it may escalate the situation.

question: Explain why factual, concise communication is particularly important in safety and environmental reports.
gold_answer: Safety and environmental reports drive concrete actions — a coastguard rebroadcast, a route change by other vessels, dispatch of a pollution response unit. Emotive or speculative language wastes airtime, complicates the coastguard's decision, and may lead to over- or under-reaction. Facts (what, where, how much, when) are what the responder needs. Concise reports also let more vessels share the channel.
expected_points: stick to what, where, how much, when
answer: Because to ensure clear and effective communication of safety information, and because to maintain compliance with safety regulations and prevent pollution, and because factual, concise communication is essential for safety and environmental reports, and because the term 'pollution' includes oil and other substances that can harm the environment.

question: Describe the role of the skipper in setting the tone for all onboard radio use.
gold_answer: The skipper is the licensed responsible operator; how they call marinas, respond to the coastguard and speak to other vessels sets the standard the rest of the crew will copy. Modelling calm, structured, courteous SMCP-style communication trains the crew implicitly and reinforces the professional culture required on a safety channel. Poor skipper example quickly becomes crew habit.
answer: The skipper sets the tone for all onboard radio use, and the officer of the watch is responsible for routine communications while on duty.

question: Explain how regular debriefs after exercises can improve crew confidence and social skills in communication.
gold_answer: A short debrief after each drill (MAYDAY, PAN PAN, marina calls) covers what went well, what was said, and what could be shorter or clearer next time. It builds the crew's confidence, corrects small phraseology errors before they become habit, and creates a shared vocabulary. Debriefs also reveal individual strengths — one crew member may be particularly calm on the radio and can lead a real call.
expected_points: identifies what worked and what to improve
builds crew confidence and shared vocabulary
reveals natural radio operators for real calls
answer: Regular debriefs after exercises are essential for effective learning, and exercises should be designed to cover all key topics.

question: Describe how to manage situations where another station is clearly using inappropriate language.
gold_answer: Do not respond in kind or engage in argument. If it is affecting safety traffic on Ch 16, the coastguard may intervene; you can note the callsign or MMSI, time and channel, and report it to the national administration (Ofcom or equivalent) or to the coastguard by phone or through a separate contact. Do not personally reprimand the offender on-air except with a brief neutral request ("Please observe correct radio procedure, out") if necessary.
expected_points: do not respond in kind or argue
report to coastguard or national administration
brief neutral request on-air if needed
answer: First, cease transmissions; Then, wait for the other station to finish; Next, do not respond if they do not notice; After that, suggest they review their language if they continue. Do this correctly and the other station may be made aware of their inappropriate language and may choose to stop using it. Just be careful: do not respond if the other station does not notice your silence.

question: Explain why unnecessary repetition or "chatter" on working channels can indirectly affect safety and environment.
gold_answer: Chatter on a working channel — long anecdotes, repeated over-explanations, small-talk between yachts — reduces the effective capacity of that channel for real vessel operations, may cause vessels to miss instructions from harbour control or race committee, and encourages migration of chat onto Ch 16 itself. Both effects can delay safety-relevant communications and, indirectly, contribute to incidents (collisions, groundings, spills).
expected_points: vessels may miss harbour or race instructions
answer: Because to ensure that the channel is not being used for emergency communications when you need it, and because to maintain effective communication and avoid interference, and because unnecessary repetition or 'chatter' on working channels can be annoying and distracting, and because this can indirectly affect safety by using valuable bandwidth.

question: Describe how a culture of professional radio use aligns with the responsibilities of a competent skipper.
gold_answer: A competent skipper is legally the responsible radio operator, sets the tone for crew and guests, and is expected by other stations (marinas, VTS, coastguard) to communicate reliably. Building a personal habit of correct pro-words, priority discipline, listening watch and courteous tone is not window-dressing but part of being a safe seafarer — it directly supports collision avoidance, SAR effectiveness and environmental protection.
expected_points: sets tone for crew and guests
expected by other stations to communicate reliably
correct pro-words, priority discipline, listening watch
part of being a safe seafarer
answer: Professional VHF radio use is essential for modern maritime operations, and a culture of respect and responsibility should be cultivated among radio users.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate how to power on the fixed VHF radio and verify it is functioning correctly.
gold_answer: Confirm the master switch to the radio is on, then press and hold the front-panel power button until the display illuminates. Verify the boot self-test completes with no error, that the MMSI or vessel name is shown, that GPS position and UTC time are displayed, and that the DSC watch indicator appears. Set to Channel 16, listen for background noise or traffic, and briefly hail a nearby station on Ch 9 or an automated test facility to confirm two-way operation.
expected_points: MMSI, GPS and DSC watch shown on display
radio check with a known station or automated test
answer: First, turn on the VHF radio; Then, check the display for signal strength and channel status; Next, listen to Channel 16 or another working channel; After that, respond if contacted by another station. Do this correctly and the VHF radio powers up and is ready for use. Just be careful: ensure the antenna is properly connected before powering on.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Show how to adjust volume and squelch for clear reception in a noisy environment.
gold_answer: With the squelch fully open (rotated to minimum) increase the volume until background noise is comfortable but audible above ambient noise. Then close the squelch by rotating it clockwise until the noise just disappears — the "threshold" point. If distant weak signals must be heard, back off the squelch a touch. Re-check volume against actual voice traffic, not just noise.
expected_points: rotate squelch clockwise until noise just disappears
back off slightly to catch weak signals
answer: First, adjust the volume; Then, adjust the squelch. Do this correctly and improved clarity of communication.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate switching between high and low power and explain when each is used.
gold_answer: Press the H/L (or 25W/1W) key on the microphone or front panel and confirm the display changes from HI to LO. Use low (1 W) inside a harbour or marina and for close-range communication (< 1 nm) with another vessel; use high (25 W) for coast station calls, offshore intership work, and any distress, urgency or safety traffic. Some coast stations force a return to high power on a specific channel.
expected_points: press H/L key on mic or front panel
low = 1 W in harbour or close range
high = 25 W for coast station, offshore, distress
answer: First, switch to high power; Then, switch back to low power. Do this correctly and improved communication range during distress situations. Just be careful: high power should only be used in emergencies.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Identify the main controls on the VHF front panel and describe their functions.
gold_answer: Typical front-panel controls: power on/off (often combined with volume knob); volume; squelch (knob or up/down keys); channel selector (rotary or up/down); H/L power key; DSC distress button (behind a red guard); Ch 16 quick-access key; menu / enter / cancel keys; and a soft-key row below the display. Behind the mic: PTT, scan/dual watch and possibly a channel keypad. Layout varies but the functions are the same on all type-approved sets.
expected_points: DSC distress button behind red guard, plus Ch 16 quick-access
answer: The VHF front panel includes controls for power, volume, squelch, and channel selection, and the power button is used to turn the radio on and off.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Show how to select a specific channel requested by the examiner.
gold_answer: Confirm the current channel set (INT/USA/CAN) matches the examiner's expected region. Rotate the channel knob or press channel up/down until the requested channel number is displayed; alternatively use the direct keypad entry (e.g. "7", "2" for Ch 72) or a soft-key shortcut. Confirm the display shows the correct channel and the appropriate simplex/duplex indicator, then listen briefly before transmitting.
expected_points: use knob, up/down or keypad entry
confirm the requested number on the display
answer: First, select the specific channel requested; Then, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by the phonetic spelling of the word or name; Next, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by the phonetic spelling again before returning to normal speech. Do this correctly and clear communication of spelled words or names over the radio.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate how to connect the VHF to a 12 V DC supply (explain or show on training rig).
gold_answer: Marine VHF sets typically require a nominal 12 V DC feed via a dedicated fused positive line (red, ≥ 5 A fuse near the battery for a 25 W set) and a direct negative return to battery negative (black). Do not tap smaller circuits. Include a battery switch or master isolator so the radio can be isolated for maintenance, and route cables away from engine and RF-noisy sources. On the training rig, connect red to +12 V, black to 0 V, and observe polarity carefully.
expected_points: dedicated fused positive line (~5 A fuse near battery)
route cables away from engine and RF-noisy sources
answer: First, connect the VHF to a 12 V DC supply; Then, switch on the VHF; Next, check the display for confirmation of power-on status. Do this correctly and the VHF radio is powered on and ready for use. Just be careful: ensure the VHF is properly connected to avoid damage.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Identify the antenna cable and explain its importance for safe radio operation.
gold_answer: The VHF antenna cable is a low-loss coaxial (typically RG-8X, RG-213 or LMR-400 for masthead runs) with a PL-259 connector at the radio and a matching antenna base. It carries the transmitted RF energy to the antenna and back-received signals to the receiver. Poor connectors, kinks or water ingress cause high VSWR, reduced range, and in extreme cases damage to the transmitter. Inspect connectors annually and re-seal any exposed joints.
expected_points: carries RF between radio and antenna
poor connectors → high VSWR and reduced range
answer: The antenna cable is essential for safe radio operation, and the antenna cable must be properly connected to the radio equipment.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate how to perform a basic radio check on an appropriate working channel.
gold_answer: Select a working channel (e.g. Ch 9 or a marina channel). Call a known station: "(station name), THIS IS (vessel name), RADIO CHECK, OVER." On reply, listen for signal report ("LOUD AND CLEAR", "READABLE WITH BACKGROUND NOISE", etc.). Thank the station and log the check. Do not perform radio checks on Ch 16 except in an emergency.
expected_points: use a working channel (Ch 9 or marina)
expect a signal report (LOUD AND CLEAR)
answer: First, set your radio to an appropriate working channel; Then, say 'Radio Check' or 'Test' three times, followed by the name of the station you are addressing; Next, wait for a response; After that, say 'Over'. Do this correctly and you will receive a response indicating whether the radio is functioning properly. Just be careful: ensure the channel is clear before initiating the check.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Show how to verify that the GPS position is available on the DSC VHF unit.
gold_answer: On the DSC VHF display, navigate to the position/status screen (or check the main screen where position and UTC time are usually shown). Confirm that latitude and longitude are displayed, that the time is current, and that no "NO GPS" or "GPS FAIL" warning appears. Cross-check position against the chart plotter. If GPS is lost, note that DSC will require manual position entry before a distress call.
expected_points: verify latitude, longitude and UTC time
no NO GPS / GPS FAIL warning
manual entry needed if GPS is lost
answer: First, select POSITION or POSITION REPORT from the menu; Then, ensure GPS position is available; Next, check for position updates every 4 minutes; After that, confirm position synchronization with the GPS. Do this correctly and accurate vessel position is communicated through DSC. Just be careful: ensure GPS connection is active for position reporting.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate how to lock and unlock the keypad or controls to prevent accidental transmissions.
gold_answer: Most sets have a KEY LOCK function accessed via a dedicated key or a menu entry. Activate it, confirm the padlock icon appears on the display, then try pressing a random key to verify no channel change or transmission occurs. To unlock, press the same key (or press-and-hold) until the padlock icon disappears. The DSC distress button under its guard normally remains active even when the keypad is locked.
expected_points: dedicated KEY LOCK key or menu entry
padlock icon on the display when active
DSC distress button typically remains active
answer: First, lock the keypad or controls; Then, unlock the keypad or controls when necessary. Do this correctly and accidental transmissions are prevented.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Show how to change channel sets (e.g., INT/USA/CAN) where equipment supports this.
gold_answer: Enter the SETUP or CHANNEL SET menu, select INT (International), USA (US Coast Guard) or CAN (Canadian) as appropriate for the operating region, and confirm the change. The active channel set is normally shown on the main display (e.g. "INT"). This affects channels with dual-mode allocations (e.g. Ch 22A only in USA). Always confirm the correct set before departure into foreign waters.
answer: First, change channel set; Then, select new channel set; Next, press 'ENTER' or 'SELECT'. Do this correctly and the radio will switch to the new channel set specified.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate correct use of the handheld microphone, including distance and speaking angle.
gold_answer: Hold the microphone about 5 cm from the mouth, slightly off-axis to avoid breath noise; grip it firmly around the PTT area to keep it steady. Press the PTT firmly, pause half a second to let the radio key up, then speak at a normal conversational volume and pace. Release the PTT immediately at the end of the message. Do not talk directly into the top of the microphone or shout.
expected_points: press PTT, pause half a second, then speak
release PTT immediately at the end
answer: First, hold the microphone two inches from your mouth; Then, speak clearly at a normal pace; Next, ensure the microphone is tilted slightly upwards; After that, maintain a vertical position when holding the microphone. Do this correctly and clear communication with other vessels or stations. Just be careful: do not hold the microphone too close to your mouth as it may distort your voice.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Show how to test the external speaker (if fitted) and adjust its volume.
gold_answer: Locate the external speaker on/off switch or the audio source selector on the front panel (some sets use a menu entry). Enable the external speaker, listen to a live channel and adjust its dedicated volume knob (or software slider) until audible in the cockpit above ambient noise but not distorted. Confirm the internal speaker is muted (or set as required). Repeat check at different helm positions.
expected_points: front-panel switch or menu entry for external speaker
enable and listen to a live channel
check audibility at all helm positions
answer: First, press the 'S' key; Then, listen for a tone; Next, if no tone is heard, check connections; After that, if still no tone, replace the speaker. Do this correctly and the speaker functions properly and alerts users of important messages. Just be careful: if no tone is heard after pressing 'S', there may be a problem with the speaker or connections.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Explain and demonstrate how to check that the emergency DSC distress button is protected (e.g., flap/guard).
gold_answer: Verify that the red DSC distress button has a spring-loaded plastic guard or a hinged flap that must be lifted before the button can be pressed. Test the guard by attempting to press through it — no distress should be initiated. Ensure that no other object (radio holder, dodger cloth) can press the guard down accidentally. Confirm the button itself operates when the guard is deliberately opened.
expected_points: red distress button with plastic guard / flap
must be lifted before button can be pressed
test that guard blocks accidental press
no object should rest against guard
button operates when guard is opened deliberately
answer: The emergency DSC distress button must be protected to prevent accidental activation, and the protection can be provided by a flap or guard covering the distress button.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate muting and un-muting of the radio if such a function exists.
gold_answer: Use the MUTE key (or menu entry) to instantly silence the loudspeaker while keeping the receiver active — useful during briefings or manoeuvring. Confirm the MUTE icon appears on the display. Press again (or select UNMUTE) to restore the audio. Do not use MUTE as a substitute for reducing volume; it is intended for short interruptions only, so critical Ch 16 traffic is not silently missed.
expected_points: silences loudspeaker while receiver stays active
not a substitute for permanent volume reduction
answer: First, mute the radio; Then, un-mute the radio. Do this correctly and the radio remains silent until the user chooses to listen again.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Show how to reset the radio after a power failure.
gold_answer: After a power failure the radio normally reboots automatically when supply is restored. Once the display is on, confirm the boot self-test passes, MMSI is present, GPS is receiving position and time, and the correct channel (Ch 16 or the last-used channel) is set. Re-enter any settings that may have reverted (channel set, brightness, volume) and log the interruption. If the radio does not restart, check the fuse and the supply voltage.
expected_points: if not restarting, check fuse and supply voltage
answer: First, turn on the radio; Then, wait for the display to show the last known status; Next, check if the DSC antenna is connected; After that, check if the VHF antenna is properly mounted; Finally, reset the radio by holding the power button until the display shows 'System Reset'; Then, wait for the system to fully reset before attempting to send or receive calls. Do this correctly and the radio will resume normal operation after a power failure. Just be careful: ensure antennas are properly connected to avoid communication issues.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate safe routing of cables to avoid damage and interference.
gold_answer: Route the power cable directly from a fused positive at the battery to the radio, keeping it away from engine and inverter cabling to reduce RF interference. Route the coaxial antenna cable on its own path, avoiding sharp bends, chafe points and hot surfaces; secure with cable ties at ≤ 300 mm spacing. Cross other cables at 90° where possible. Ensure all cables are protected where they pass through bulkheads (grommets) and check annually for chafe.
expected_points: dedicated fused power cable direct from battery
antenna coax on its own path, no sharp bends
cross other cables at 90° where possible
grommets at bulkheads, annual chafe check
answer: First, route cables along the hull; Then, secure cables with cable ties or clamps; Next, protect cables from abrasion; After that, ensure cables are not in contact with hot surfaces; Finally, maintain a clear space around the cable glands; Then, check cables regularly for damage. Do this correctly and reduced risk of cable failure due to improper routing. Just be careful: cables must not be routed over hot surfaces.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Explain and, if possible, demonstrate how to power the radio from an alternative battery or power source.
gold_answer: If the main service bank is depleted, the radio can normally be switched over to a separate emergency/domestic battery via the vessel's battery selector, or connected directly to a small dedicated emergency battery through a fused lead. Confirm 12 V nominal supply, check that the radio boots normally and that GPS is still available. On the training rig, disconnect the primary battery lead and connect the emergency lead in the same way, observing polarity and fuse rating.
expected_points: battery selector or dedicated emergency battery
radio boots and GPS still available
note any loss of GPS if it draws from another bus
answer: First, connect an external power supply; Then, ensure the power source is compatible with the radio's requirements; Next, monitor the power connection for any issues. Do this correctly and the radio will operate reliably without relying solely on its internal battery. Just be careful: ensure the power source is properly rated to avoid damage to the radio.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Show how to verify that the correct channel list (for the operating region) is available on the set.
gold_answer: On the main display check the channel set indicator (INT, USA or CAN). Cycle through a few characteristic channels (e.g. Ch 22A, Ch 67, Ch 80) and confirm that they are present and correctly labelled for the region. If the set has a menu of channel groups (Atlantic, US, Canada) verify the correct one is selected. Cross-check against the almanac's channel list for the current operating area.
expected_points: check channel set indicator on the display
select correct channel group if applicable
answer: First, ensure the correct channel list for the operating region is available; Then, select the appropriate channel configuration; Next, verify the selected channels match the required working channels; After that, check if the DSC function is operational; Finally, confirm the antenna system is properly connected; Then, ensure the antenna switch operates correctly; Then, verify the antenna impedance matches 50 ohms; Then, check the antenna height above sea level; Then, confirm the antenna radiation pattern is as specified. Do this correctly and successful operation of VHF radio communication.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate shutting down the radio correctly while leaving it ready for the next operation.
gold_answer: Ensure Ch 16 (or the intended standby channel) is set, volume is at a normal level and squelch at threshold. Note the last known GPS position and UTC time in the log. Press and hold the power key until the display switches off. Verify no residual glow and that the DSC guard flap is closed. When the master switch is turned off, the settings will be preserved for the next start-up.
expected_points: set channel to Ch 16 before shutdown
normal volume and squelch at threshold
note position and UTC time in the log
press and hold power key to switch off
answer: First, set the radio to Channel 16 or the intended standby channel; Then, leave the volume at a normal level; Next, ensure the squelch is set to the correct position; After that, leave the power on unless instructed otherwise; Finally, shut down only when preparing for an extended rest or shutdown. Do this correctly and the radio remains operational and ready for immediate use upon next activation. Just be careful: do not turn off the radio if you plan to use it soon.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Identify all components of the ship's radio installation: transceiver, antenna, power supply, GPS input, etc.
gold_answer: Point to and name each item: fixed VHF transceiver at the chart table; masthead VHF/DSC antenna; low-loss coaxial run and PL-259 connector; DC feed with fuse near the battery (typically 5–10 A) and battery isolator; GPS antenna or plotter feeding NMEA 0183/2000 to the radio; external cockpit speaker if fitted; DSC ground/RF earth. Confirm labels, cable runs and the ship station licence document held on board.
expected_points: fused DC feed and battery isolator
external cockpit speaker and ship station licence
answer: The ship's radio installation must include a DSC controller, and the installation may also include a GPS receiver and a backup power source.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to check the ship station's MMSI is correctly programmed into the DSC VHF.
gold_answer: On the DSC menu select 'MY MMSI' or 'STATION ID'. Confirm the nine-digit MMSI shown matches the ship station licence. Cross-check the first three digits (MID) against the flag state code — UK 232/233/234/235, Netherlands 244/245/246. If the MMSI is missing, showing 000000000 or the wrong number, do not send any DSC calls and note the issue; on most sets the MMSI can only be entered once and requires a manufacturer reset to change.
expected_points: MY MMSI or STATION ID menu entry
match to the ship station licence
note issue if missing or wrong
answer: First, check the ship station's MMSI; Then, program the correct MMSI if it is incorrect; Next, verify the MMSI is correctly programmed after 24 hours. Do this correctly and the DSC VHF system will function correctly for distress alerts. Just be careful: if the MMSI is incorrect, distress alerts may not be received by the intended rescue coordination centre.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to scroll through menu options to access DSC functions.
gold_answer: Press the MENU key or dedicated DSC key. Use the up/down channel keys or the rotary knob to scroll through the top-level entries — typically DISTRESS, INDIVIDUAL CALL, GROUP CALL, ALL SHIPS, MSI/POSITION REPORT, LOG. Press ENTER or the soft key labelled OK to open the selected item. ESC returns to the previous level. Practise navigating without transmitting until the layout is familiar.
expected_points: scroll with knob or up/down keys
top-level entries: DISTRESS, INDIVIDUAL, GROUP, ALL SHIPS, LOG
ENTER / soft key to open, ESC to go back
answer: First, press the 'DSC' key; Then, scroll through menu options using arrow keys; Next, select desired function using 'ENTER'. Do this correctly and successful navigation to DSC functions for distress alerts and safety communications.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate setting up an individual DSC routine call to a specified MMSI.
gold_answer: Open DSC menu → INDIVIDUAL CALL → ROUTINE. Enter the target MMSI digit by digit (or select from the directory), then choose the proposed voice working channel (e.g. Ch 72). Press SEND / CALL. Wait for the receiving radio to acknowledge; both radios switch to the working channel. Then follow up by voice: "(other vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER."
expected_points: voice follow-up on the agreed channel
answer: First, set up an individual DSC routine call; Then, wait for the called station to acknowledge and establish voice communication on channel 16 or a working channel. Do this correctly and successful establishment of communication with the specified station.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to acknowledge a received routine DSC call and switch to the indicated working channel.
gold_answer: When a routine DSC call is received, the radio alarms, displays the caller's MMSI and the proposed channel. Press ACCEPT / ACK (or the soft key labelled ACK/ACCEPT). The radio automatically switches to the proposed channel; listen briefly, then reply by voice: "(caller), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL (…), OVER." If the channel is unsuitable, press REJECT and call the station manually on an alternative channel.
expected_points: radio alarms and displays MMSI and channel
voice reply on the working channel
answer: First, acknowledge the DSC call; Then, switch to the indicated working channel; Next, set the transmitter power to 25W; After that, transmit 'Mayday, Mayday, Mayday' three times; Finally, state your vessel name, position, and nature of distress; Then, end with 'Over'. Do this correctly and the distress message is communicated effectively to relevant parties. Just be careful: ensure the transmitter is set to 25W for optimal range.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to set and confirm the vessel's position manually on the radio if GPS input fails.
gold_answer: On the DSC/position menu select MANUAL POSITION or POSITION ENTRY. Enter latitude (degrees, minutes and hemisphere N/S) and longitude (degrees, minutes and hemisphere E/W), plus the UTC time of the position, using the keypad. Save and confirm the entry — the radio now displays "MAN" or "USER" next to the position instead of "GPS". Update the manual position every few minutes while GPS is unavailable.
expected_points: enter UTC time of the position
display shows MAN or USER indicator
update every few minutes while GPS is unavailable
answer: First, set the vessel's position manually; Then, confirm the position by keying the PTT button and saying 'position confirmed'. Do this correctly and the vessel's position is accurately communicated to other stations.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to view the DSC call log and identify the last received alert.
gold_answer: On the DSC menu open LOG or CALL LOG; select RECEIVED (or DISTRESS / URGENCY / SAFETY / ROUTINE as needed). Scroll to the most recent entry, press ENTER to view details: sender MMSI, category, time (UTC), position and follow-up channel. This lets the operator review missed alerts or reconstruct events after the fact. Some sets separate received and transmitted logs.
expected_points: most recent entry at the top
details: MMSI, category, time, position, channel
answer: First, press 'DSC Log' or select 'DSC Log' from the menu; Then, scroll through the log entries; Next, find the last alert received; After that, note the MMSI and time of the last alert. Do this correctly and you can review recent DSC communications and identify important alerts. Just be careful: ensure the DSC is properly configured to receive alerts.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate switching between intership and port operation channels according to instructions.
gold_answer: Take the examiner's instruction ("switch to Ch 12 for port control") and select the channel using knob, up/down or keypad entry. Confirm the display shows the new number and that low power is selected if in a harbour. Announce the switch on the current channel first ("...GOING TO CHANNEL ONE TWO, OVER"), then on the new channel re-establish contact briefly.
expected_points: listen to the examiner's channel instruction
answer: First, switch to the required channel; Then, listen for 1 minute; Next, acknowledge the incoming call if on the same channel; After that, switch back to the original channel after 2 minutes. Do this correctly and successful communication with the intended station.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to adjust display brightness for day and night operations.
gold_answer: Use the BRIGHTNESS or DIM key (often a dedicated key or a short-press of the power button). Set full brightness in daylight so the display is readable under the spray hood; at night reduce brightness to preserve night vision but keep essential icons (channel number, DSC alarm) visible. Modern sets have a NIGHT MODE preset that also switches the backlight colour to red or amber.
expected_points: BRIGHTNESS / DIM key or short-press power
reduce at night for night vision
NIGHT MODE preset on modern sets
answer: First, adjust display brightness; Then, select night mode. Do this correctly and improved visibility during day and night operations.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to test an internal speaker and any external loudspeaker if present.
gold_answer: Tune to a live channel with regular traffic (e.g. Ch 16 or a marina channel). Adjust internal volume and confirm audio is clear. Enable the external cockpit speaker (dedicated switch or menu) and adjust its volume, checking audibility at the helm and around the cockpit. Toggle between speakers to verify each works independently. If neither produces audio, check the AF/GAIN and check the speaker connector.
answer: First, press the 'TONE' or 'SPEAKER TEST' button; Then, listen for a tone from all speakers; Next, check each external speaker's power cable connection; After that, verify fuse status; Finally, replace blown fuses; Then, seek professional assistance if problems persist. Do this correctly and all speakers will produce sound during testing. Just be careful: ensure all connections are secure to prevent speaker failure.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to select and call a coast station using DSC from an onboard directory (if fitted).
gold_answer: Open DSC → DIRECTORY, select the coast station entry (e.g. HM COASTGUARD), which stores the coast station's MMSI. From there choose INDIVIDUAL CALL → ROUTINE, choose the voice working channel used by the coast station (e.g. Ch 67 for UK coastguard) and press SEND. When the coast station acknowledges, follow up by voice on the working channel.
expected_points: choose the coast station's voice working channel
answer: First, scroll through the directory until the desired coast station is highlighted; Then, press the 'CALL' key; Next, wait for the coast station to respond; After that, read out the MMSI number and call sign when prompted. Do this correctly and successful establishment of communication with the coast station.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to initiate a DSC test call where this is permitted (on simulator, not live).
gold_answer: On the training simulator open DSC → TEST CALL. Enter the target MMSI (typically a coast station MMSI that supports automatic DSC test replies) and press SEND. The simulator sends the test call and waits for the acknowledgement, which is displayed on the log. Live DSC test calls should only be made against stations that offer this service; misuse can cause SAR confusion.
expected_points: target MMSI (coast station that supports test)
live tests only against supporting stations
answer: First, select the appropriate menu option for DSC self-test; Then, follow the on-screen instructions for the self-test procedure; Next, note the result of the self-test and take appropriate action if specified. Do this correctly and successful completion of the DSC self-test indicates proper system functionality. Just be careful: failure to perform regular DSC self-tests may lead to system failures during critical operations.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to cancel an outgoing routine DSC call before it is sent.
gold_answer: During the composition step (after selecting the call type and before pressing SEND), press ESC / CANCEL to abort the call. If the SEND button has already been pressed but the radio is still in the pre-transmission countdown (some sets show a short delay), press CANCEL again — many DSC sets will still block the transmission. Once transmitted, the call cannot be recalled and, if incorrect, must be corrected by a follow-up call.
expected_points: also works during short pre-transmit countdown
correct by a follow-up call if needed
answer: First, press the PTT button; Then, select 'Cancel' from the menu; Next, confirm the cancellation. Do this correctly and the routine DSC call will be canceled before transmission. Just be careful: ensure the call is not yet transmitted to avoid wasting resources.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to configure a group call using a given group MMSI (if supported by equipment).
gold_answer: Open DSC → GROUP CALL → SETUP (or DIRECTORY entry for the group). Enter the nine-digit group MMSI (starting with a leading zero, e.g. 023201234) and store it under a memorable name (e.g. FLOTILLA-2026). To make the group call, select GROUP CALL → send, choose the working channel, and transmit. All correctly programmed radios alert and can switch to the working channel together.
expected_points: GROUP CALL SETUP or DIRECTORY entry
group MMSI starts with a leading zero
all group radios alert and can switch
answer: First, scroll through the directory or enter the group MMSI; Then, select the group and press the PTT button; Next, speak your message. Do this correctly and all stations in the group receive the call simultaneously.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to access and interpret stored DSC distress alerts on the device.
gold_answer: Open DSC → LOG → RECEIVED DISTRESS. Scroll to select an entry and press ENTER to view: sender's MMSI (identifies the vessel), UTC time, nature of distress if selected, position, and follow-up channel. Cross-check MMSI against the vessel directory if available. Use the log to reconstruct incident history for the coastguard or an inquiry.
expected_points: details: MMSI, time, nature, position, channel
answer: First, press DISTRESS button; Then, scroll through distress alerts; Next, read detailed information of each alert. Do this correctly and the user can review all received distress alerts and access detailed information about each one.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to temporarily disable DSC audible alarms and then re-enable them correctly.
gold_answer: When an alarm sounds, press the ALARM CANCEL / SILENCE key to mute the tone for the current alert while keeping the DSC watch active. To disable all alarms globally is generally not permitted on type-approved sets — but volume can be reduced via the DSC audio volume setting. Always re-check that the alarm is re-enabled at full volume immediately after the temporary silencing, so the next alert is heard.
expected_points: ALARM CANCEL / SILENCE for current alert only
cannot globally disable on type-approved sets
reduce alarm volume via DSC audio setting
answer: First, press the SSB button; Then, hold the SSB button until the tone stops; Next, lift the cover over the SSB button; After that, press the red cross on the cover; Finally, replace the cover and press it down; Then, wait 5 seconds; Then, press the SSB button again; Then, hold the SSB button for 2 seconds. Do this correctly and DSC audible alarms will be temporarily disabled. Just be careful: do not touch the antenna during an alarm.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to confirm the ship station is configured for Sea Area A1 operation.
gold_answer: Confirm the VHF/DSC set is powered, has GPS input, is on Ch 70 DSC watch and Ch 16 voice watch, and that the MMSI matches the ship station licence. For Sea Area A1 the DSC-VHF combination plus (recommended) an EPIRB is sufficient — no MF/HF or Inmarsat is required. Cross-check the ship station licence entry showing 'A1' or equivalent.
expected_points: DSC watch on Ch 70 and voice watch on Ch 16
no MF/HF or Inmarsat required for A1
answer: First, confirm ship station is configured for Sea Area A1 operation; Then, ensure DSC is set to transmit on 70 channels. Do this correctly and successful confirmation of ship station configuration for A1 operation.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to access context-sensitive help or quick menus if available on the radio.
gold_answer: Many modern sets have a HELP or ? soft key that shows a short description of the currently selected menu entry. Others provide quick menus via a long-press on a specific key. Demonstrate opening one such menu on the training rig, review the visible options, and explain how to use the built-in help to remind the operator of DSC steps without needing the paper manual.
expected_points: HELP or ? soft key on many sets
long-press for quick menu on others
supports DSC step reminders under stress
answer: First, press the HELP key; Then, read the displayed text and follow the instructions. Do this correctly and improved understanding of radio functions.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to check the supply voltage as displayed by the radio (if such a feature exists).
gold_answer: On the STATUS or DIAGNOSTIC menu of many modern radios the current supply voltage is displayed. Note the value — a nominal reading is 12.6–13.8 V under charge, and below 11 V the radio may reset during a distress transmission. If the voltage is low, investigate the battery bank, fuses and cabling before departure. If the feature does not exist, use the vessel's battery monitor as a proxy.
expected_points: STATUS / DIAGNOSTIC menu shows supply voltage
investigate battery, fuses, cabling if low
use vessel battery monitor if no on-radio feature
answer: First, check the supply voltage; Then, check the fuse(s); Next, replace the fuse(s) if blown; After that, seek professional assistance if problems persist. Do this correctly and the radio will function properly. Just be careful: do not exceed the specified voltage or current ratings.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate and explain the correct use of any integrated AIS display functionality related to communications, if present.
gold_answer: On radios with integrated AIS the operator can view a list of nearby AIS targets by MMSI, name, CPA and TCPA. Selecting a target lets the operator send a DSC individual call directly to that vessel's MMSI (useful for coordinating a passing manoeuvre with a large ship). Demonstrate opening the AIS list, selecting one target, and initiating an INDIVIDUAL CALL from it. Confirm the correct MMSI is loaded into the DSC call.
expected_points: AIS target list with MMSI and name
select target to send DSC individual call
confirms MMSI in the call setup
useful for passing arrangements with commercial traffic
answer: First, select the appropriate channel; Then, press the transmit button; Next, speak clearly in English at a pace of 120 wpm; After that, ensure the volume is set appropriately; Finally, monitor the channel for safety communications. Do this correctly and effective communication with other vessels and shore stations. Just be careful: do not transmit false distress or urgency calls.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to switch the handheld VHF on and off.
gold_answer: To switch on, press and hold the power button (usually combined with the volume knob) for 1–2 seconds until the display lights up and the boot self-test completes. To switch off, press and hold the same button for 2–3 seconds until the display fades. Confirm any battery-low warning at start-up. Do not simply pull the battery — the settings need a clean shutdown to be preserved.
expected_points: power button (often combined with volume knob)
press and hold to switch on
press and hold longer to switch off
answer: First, turn on the handheld VHF; Then, hold the power button until the display lights up; Next, turn off the handheld VHF; After that, press and hold the power button until the display goes dark. Do this correctly and the handheld VHF is powered on or off as needed.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to check the battery charge level on a handheld unit.
gold_answer: The display normally shows a small battery icon divided into segments. Full segments indicate full charge; one or two segments indicate imminent low-battery. Some handhelds also show voltage in the STATUS menu. A separate BATTERY TEST option, where fitted, briefly loads the battery and reports capacity. If low, replace the battery pack or place the unit on the charger and use the other handheld for the current watch.
expected_points: battery icon with segments on display
one or two segments = low battery
voltage in STATUS menu on some sets
replace or charge if low, use backup for watch
answer: First, turn on the radio; Then, check the battery charge level; Next, ensure the antenna is properly connected; After that, perform a transmit test; Finally, check the speaker or headphones for sound. Do this correctly and the radio functions properly and can be used effectively. Just be careful: ensure the antenna is fully extended before transmitting.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to change channels on the handheld.
gold_answer: Use the up/down channel keys, the rotary knob or the direct keypad entry (where fitted). Confirm the new channel number on the display. On many handhelds a dedicated Ch 16 (or Ch 16/9) key returns instantly to the calling channel. Confirm the correct channel set (INT/USA/CAN) matches the region of operation.
answer: First, press the 'Channel' button; Then, scroll through the list of available channels using the up and down keys; Next, select the desired channel by pressing 'Enter' or 'Send'. Do this correctly and the handheld radio will switch to the selected channel.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to set the handheld to high or low power and explain when each should be used.
gold_answer: Press the H/L key (or its soft-menu equivalent) to toggle between high (typically 5–6 W) and low (typically 1 W) power. Use high power for offshore calls, coast station contact and any distress or urgency traffic; use low power inside a marina, alongside another vessel or when talking to nearby crew ashore. Low power both saves battery and reduces interference on shared channels.
expected_points: high ~5–6 W for offshore and distress
low ~1 W in marina, short range
answer: First, set the handheld to high power; Then, set the handheld to low power. Do this correctly and improved range for communication in open water. Just be careful: high power settings may not be necessary for close-range communication.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate adjusting volume and squelch on the handheld radio.
gold_answer: Rotate the volume knob (often combined with the power button) or use the volume up/down keys until traffic is audible over background noise. Rotate the squelch knob (or menu entry) fully open, then gradually close until the background noise just disappears ("squelch threshold"). If reception of a distant station is expected, back off the squelch slightly. Re-check with a real transmission where possible.
expected_points: open squelch fully then close to threshold
answer: First, adjust the volume; Then, adjust the squelch. Do this correctly and improved clarity in communication.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to attach and secure the handheld's antenna.
gold_answer: Align the antenna's BNC or SMA thread with the handheld's connector, screw or push-lock it fully home, and confirm no play or wobble. Never transmit without the antenna attached — this can damage the transmitter output stage. Inspect the antenna for cracks, corrosion or a bent base and replace if damaged. For range use the supplied full-length antenna rather than a short 'stubby' where possible.
expected_points: BNC or SMA connector, fully home
inspect for cracks, corrosion, bent base
answer: First, attach the handheld's antenna; Then, secure the antenna. Do this correctly and improved communication range and quality. Just be careful: ensure the antenna is properly secured to avoid damage.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate correct microphone and speaker positioning on the handheld while speaking.
gold_answer: Hold the handheld vertically or at a slight angle away from the body, with the microphone (usually behind the front-panel grille) about 5 cm from the mouth and slightly off-axis. Speak at a normal conversational volume. During reception, hold the speaker close to the ear or angled towards the operator to hear over ambient noise. Do not cover the antenna with your hand — it detunes the signal.
expected_points: hold vertically or slight angle away from body
mic ~5 cm from mouth, slightly off-axis
answer: First, hold the microphone at least 2 cm from your mouth; Then, speak clearly and slowly; Next, keep the microphone vertical when transmitting; After that, position the speaker near your ear when listening; Finally, hold the handheld horizontally when holding it in one hand; Then, hold the handheld vertically when holding it in two hands. Do this correctly and clear communication is achieved. Just be careful: do not hold the microphone too close to your mouth or too far away.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to select channel 16 and then return to a previously used working channel.
gold_answer: Press the dedicated Ch 16 (or 16/9) key to jump directly to Channel 16 — this works from any other channel. To return to the previously used channel, press the same key again (many handhelds toggle back to the last channel used), or use LAST CHANNEL / RECALL if provided, or manually re-select the channel. Confirm the new channel number on the display each time.
expected_points: dedicated Ch 16 key for instant access
press again or use LAST CHANNEL to toggle back
answer: First, press the '16' button; Then, hold the transmit key and say 'I switch to channel one-six, over'; Next, switch back to the working channel. Do this correctly and the operator successfully switches to channel 16 for distress calls and returns to the working channel.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to operate any waterproofing seals or covers (e.g., for charging ports).
gold_answer: Locate the rubber flap covering the charging or accessory port. Open by lifting the flap gently at the tab (not the connector itself); after use, press the flap firmly into its seat until it clicks / seats flush. Inspect the seal for dirt, sand or damage before closing — a compromised seal is a common cause of water ingress. After sea use rinse the handheld with fresh water with the flap closed.
expected_points: open by lifting tab, not connector
press firmly back into seat until flush
inspect seal for dirt and damage
rinse in fresh water with flap closed after sea use
answer: First, ensure all waterproofing seals and covers are in place; Then, check the integrity of waterproofing materials; Next, replace damaged or compromised seals. Do this correctly and equipment remains protected from water damage. Just be careful: failure to maintain waterproofing can lead to water ingress and potential equipment failure.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to secure the handheld to prevent loss overboard (lanyard, clip, etc.).
gold_answer: Attach the supplied wrist lanyard to the eyelet on the handheld and loop it around the wrist during use. When stowed, use the belt clip and clip to the harness or a lifejacket lanyard point. Consider a floating case for extra buoyancy. Do not carry a handheld loose in a pocket without a secondary tether. Regularly check the eyelet and lanyard for wear.
expected_points: belt clip to harness or lifejacket
never loose in pocket without tether
check eyelet and lanyard for wear
answer: First, mount the handheld on a fixed mount; Then, use a lanyard or clip to secure it; Next, stow it in a dedicated padded case. Do this correctly and the handheld is protected from water and accidental drops. Just be careful: do not stow the handheld in a cargo hold or locker without proper protection.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate the charging procedure for the handheld battery.
gold_answer: Insert the battery pack into the correct orientation on the charging cradle (or plug the charging cable into the handheld's charging port) and connect the charger to the 12 V or mains supply. Verify the charging indicator LED (usually red = charging, green = full). Do not charge in extreme temperatures. Once fully charged, disconnect and store the handheld ready for the next watch — some Li-ion chemistries prefer partial rather than 100% charge for storage.
expected_points: connect charger to 12 V or mains
LED indicators for charging and full
disconnect and store ready for next watch
answer: First, charge the handheld battery; Then, check the charge level of the handheld battery; Next, charge the base station battery; After that, check the charge level of the base station battery. Do this correctly and the handheld and base station batteries will be fully charged and ready for use. Just be careful: do not charge the batteries in direct sunlight or near heat sources.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to change a battery pack safely on the handheld unit.
gold_answer: Switch the handheld off. Release the battery-pack latch (a lever, screw or slide depending on the model) and pull the pack straight off the back. Check the contacts on both battery and handheld for cleanliness and no corrosion. Fit the new pack in the correct orientation, confirming the latch clicks home. Power on and confirm normal operation, then log the swap.
expected_points: fit new pack in correct orientation
power on and confirm normal operation
answer: First, turn off the radio; Then, remove the battery pack; Next, wait for 5 minutes before reinserting the battery pack; After that, reinsert the battery pack and turn on the radio. Do this correctly and the radio will function properly after the battery pack is reinserted. Just be careful: do not touch the metal contacts of the battery pack while it is being removed or inserted.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to perform a radio check using the handheld from deck.
gold_answer: On deck, extend the antenna vertically, select an appropriate working channel (e.g. Ch 9 or a marina channel), and call a known station: "(station), THIS IS (own vessel handheld), RADIO CHECK, OVER." Wait for the signal report. Repeat with the fixed radio for comparison. Do not use Ch 16. Note that handheld range is much lower than the masthead antenna's — do not expect the same report.
expected_points: compare with fixed radio; range naturally lower
answer: First, hold the PTT button and say 'Radio Check'; Then, listen for a response; Next, say 'This is [vessel name], over'. Do this correctly and you will receive a response if the radio is working properly.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to use any available scan or dual-watch function on the handheld.
gold_answer: Access SCAN or DW/TRI-WATCH via a dedicated key or menu. Scan cycles through all channels stored in the scan list, pausing on any active channel. Dual-watch monitors Ch 16 (or the priority channel) plus one selected working channel simultaneously — useful when waiting for a marina call while at anchor. Turn scan off before transmitting, since scan is paused during PTT.
expected_points: SCAN cycles through all stored channels
DW / TRI-WATCH monitors Ch 16 plus working channel
use DW at anchor waiting for a marina
answer: First, press the Scan button; Then, hold down the Scan button until the display shows 'Scan On'; Next, release the Scan button when ready. Do this correctly and the radio will automatically monitor multiple channels for incoming calls.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to reduce squelch temporarily to check for weak signals.
gold_answer: Rotate the squelch knob anti-clockwise (or press the monitor button, where fitted) so the squelch fully opens — background noise (hiss) is heard. Listen for a few seconds; any faint voice traffic will now be audible. Once satisfied, return the squelch to threshold. Do not leave the squelch open — continuous noise fatigues the operator and drains the battery on receive.
expected_points: rotate squelch anti-clockwise or press MONITOR
do not leave squelch open (fatigue, battery drain)
answer: First, set the squelch control to its maximum; Then, gradually turn it down until static is heard; Next, adjust further if necessary for weak signals. Do this correctly and improved reception of weak signals.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to stow the handheld correctly when not in use to protect it from damage.
gold_answer: Switch off, close any port flaps and secure the antenna. Stow in a dedicated wall-mount holder or a padded soft case in a dry, ventilated locker near the companionway — accessible in an emergency but protected from spray, sun and impact. Do not stow in a pocket with loose keys, or near strong magnets. Charge fully before stowing for long periods.
expected_points: switch off and close port flaps
answer: First, stow the handheld in a padded case or in a dedicated pocket; Then, wrap the antenna in protective material before stowing; Next, secure the power cable and data cable if applicable. Do this correctly and the handheld is protected from physical damage and environmental factors. Just be careful: do not store the handheld in direct sunlight or near heat sources.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate using the handheld for intership communication between two training vessels.
gold_answer: On the calling channel (Ch 16 or agreed Ch 9), call the other vessel three times, THIS IS your vessel three times, OVER. Agree an intership working channel (e.g. Ch 72), both switch and re-establish contact. Use low power for close range, keep the message brief, and close with OUT once done. Return listening watch to Ch 16 on both handhelds.
expected_points: use low power for close range
answer: First, switch on the handheld VHF radio; Then, set the handheld to Channel 16 or the desired working channel; Next, hold the PTT button and speak clearly into the microphone; After that, ensure the volume is turned up; Finally, listen carefully for responses; Then, switch off the radio when finished. Do this correctly and successful communication with another vessel. Just be careful: ensure proper pronunciation of numbers and place names to avoid confusion.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to clean contacts and seals on the handheld unit if needed.
gold_answer: Remove the battery. Wipe the metal battery-pack and handheld contacts with a soft dry cloth or a cotton bud very lightly moistened with isopropyl alcohol — never abrasive material. Inspect and gently clean the rubber flap seals with fresh water and a soft cloth; check for cracks or missing rubber. Re-fit the battery only when everything is dry, and confirm normal power-on.
expected_points: soft dry cloth or isopropyl on cotton bud
clean rubber seals with fresh water
answer: First, turn the handheld unit upside down and tap it gently; Then, use compressed air or a soft brush to remove debris; Next, wipe the exterior with a soft, dry cloth; After that, apply a thin layer of silicone grease to the rubber seals; Finally, inspect the seals for cracks or deterioration; Then, replace seals if damaged. Do this correctly and the handheld unit functions properly without interference. Just be careful: do not use abrasive materials or solvents when cleaning.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to check that the handheld is set to the correct channel set (INT/USA/CAN, if present).
gold_answer: Open the SETUP or CHANNEL SET menu, note the currently selected channel set (INT, USA, CAN) on the main display, and change if required. Verify by scrolling to a characteristic channel — e.g. Ch 22A should exist only in USA, Ch 88 in INT. Confirm the change persists after power-cycle. Choosing the wrong channel set is one of the most common cross-border errors.
expected_points: current set shown on main display
answer: First, ensure the handheld is set to the correct channel set; Then, check the display for the current channel and frequency. Do this correctly and the user will be able to communicate on the appropriate channel for their location.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Explain and demonstrate the limitations of range when using the handheld from different points on the vessel.
gold_answer: Handheld range is limited by antenna height and body absorption. From the cockpit at deck level (~1 m) expect 3–5 nm to another handheld; from the mast steps (~5 m) up to 8–10 nm; below decks the range drops sharply. Position the operator with a clear view towards the intended recipient, keep the antenna vertical, and hold the handheld away from body and metal structures. Do not rely on a handheld for offshore distress alerting.
expected_points: range limited by antenna height and body absorption
not a substitute for fixed VHF offshore
answer: The handheld VHF radio has a range of approximately 3 to 5 nautical miles to other handhelds, and the range decreases if either unit is moved further apart.

question: On a simulator, demonstrate sending a DSC distress alert with correct category and position.
gold_answer: On the simulator open DSC → DISTRESS. Select the nature of distress (e.g. SINKING, FIRE, COLLISION) if time allows; otherwise leave as UNDESIGNATED. Confirm GPS position is present. Lift the guard flap and press and hold the red distress button until the confirmation tone (typically 3–5 seconds). The simulator sends the alert on Ch 70 with MMSI, position, time and category, then automatically switches to Ch 16 for the voice follow-up.
expected_points: select nature of distress if time
press and hold the red button 3–5 s
auto-switch to Ch 16 for voice follow-up
answer: First, select the appropriate category for the distress alert; Then, transmit the distress alert using DSC; Next, ensure the position is transmitted if not included in the DSC alert. Do this correctly and the distress alert is successfully sent to all stations within range. Just be careful: ensure the distress alert is only sent when there is an actual emergency.

question: Immediately after, perform the associated MAYDAY voice call on the designated voice channel.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 transmit: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS (vessel name x3), MMSI (…), CALLSIGN (…), MAYDAY (vessel name), POSITION (lat/long or bearing/distance from a fixed point), NATURE OF DISTRESS (e.g. sinking after collision), ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, (…) POB, ADDITIONAL INFORMATION (safety equipment on board), OVER." Speak slowly and clearly.
expected_points: THIS IS + vessel name x3, MMSI/callsign
answer: A DSC distress alert includes the position of the distressed vessel, and a voice MAYDAY call should be made on Channel 16 or 2182 kHz after sending a DSC distress alert.

question: Demonstrate repeating the MAYDAY call after no response is heard for a specified period.
gold_answer: If no acknowledgement is heard within about 15 seconds, repeat the full MAYDAY call unchanged. If still no answer after several attempts, repeat again from the DSC — some sets automatically retransmit the DSC distress alert every few minutes until acknowledged. Continue monitoring Ch 16 and Ch 70 between calls. If a coast station is unreachable, transmit MAYDAY RELAY on behalf of yourself as if you were a third party (some SRC procedures teach a modified relay).
expected_points: monitor Ch 16 and Ch 70 between calls
MAYDAY RELAY if coast station out of range
answer: First, repeat the full MAYDAY call after four minutes; Then, do not send further distress messages unless a general broadcast is required. Do this correctly and increased chances of receiving assistance due to repeated calls. Just be careful: do not send further distress messages unless a general broadcast is required.

question: Show how to respond by voice to a MAYDAY call from another vessel as a nearby ship offering assistance.
gold_answer: Wait to let the coast station or MRCC acknowledge first. If no acknowledgement is heard after a reasonable interval (~5 minutes in Sea Area A1) and you can help, transmit on Ch 16: "(distress vessel name), THIS IS (own vessel), RECEIVED MAYDAY, MY POSITION (…), ETA TO YOUR POSITION (…), STATE OF READINESS (…), OVER." Continue to keep the MRCC informed once they take control.
expected_points: offer assistance if no ACK after ~5 minutes
cooperate with MRCC once they take control
answer: First, respond promptly to the MAYDAY call; Then, maintain communication with the distress vessel; Next, assist in any way possible. Do this correctly and the distressed vessel receives timely assistance. Just be careful: do not ignore a MAYDAY call.

question: Demonstrate how to acknowledge a distress relay from a coast station without interfering with control of traffic.
gold_answer: When a coast station issues MAYDAY RELAY, remain silent unless specifically called. If you can assist and the coast station invites acknowledgement, transmit: "(coast station), THIS IS (own vessel), RECEIVED MAYDAY RELAY OF (time UTC), MY POSITION (…), READY TO ASSIST, OVER." Do not attempt to acknowledge to the distress vessel directly — the coast station is in control.
expected_points: acknowledge only to the controlling coast station
state received MAYDAY RELAY and time
do not talk directly to the distress vessel
answer: First, acknowledge the distress relay; Then, ensure the coast station has the vessel's position and traffic situation; Next, wait for further instructions from the coast station. Do this correctly and the coast station will provide further instructions regarding the distress situation. Just be careful: do not interfere with the control of traffic while awaiting further instructions.

question: Show the correct use of the phrase SEELONCE MAYDAY under examiner guidance.
gold_answer: The distress vessel or the controlling coast station may impose silence on the channel: "SEELONCE MAYDAY, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS (vessel), SEELONCE MAYDAY, OUT."
