Then only the distress vessel, the controlling station and specifically requested assisting stations may transmit. Silence is lifted with SEELONCE FEENEE (silence lifted) or partially relaxed with PRUDONCE (limited resumption). Note pronunciation: SAY-LONSS MAY-DEE.
expected_points: imposed by distress vessel or controlling coast station
SEELONCE MAYDAY, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS ..., SEELONCE MAYDAY, OUT
only distress and controlling stations may transmit
answer: The phrase 'SEELONCE MAYDAY' is used to indicate the start of a distress alert, and the phrase 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY' should be repeated every four minutes until a response is received.

question: Demonstrate cancelling a false DSC distress alert on the simulator and then issuing a MAYDAY CANCELLED voice message.
gold_answer: On the simulator use DSC → DISTRESS CANCEL if available. Then on Ch 16 transmit: "ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel name x3, MMSI), POSITION (…), CANCEL MY DISTRESS ALERT OF (UTC time), REASON (e.g. inadvertent activation), NO ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, THIS IS (vessel), OUT." Confirm the cancellation with the coast station and log the event with time, reason and coast station response.
expected_points: ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS + vessel + MMSI
CANCEL MY DISTRESS ALERT OF (UTC time) with reason
confirm with coast station and log

question: Show how to log the key details of a distress communication (time, position, vessel name, nature of distress).
gold_answer: In the radio or deck log record: UTC time of the initial alert, channel used (Ch 70 DSC + Ch 16 voice), sender's MMSI/callsign and name, position (lat/long), nature of distress, POB, coast station involved, key MRCC instructions, and time of cancellation or termination. Keep entries factual and chronological. The log may later be reviewed by the coastguard or an inquiry.
expected_points: MRCC instructions and time of termination

question: Demonstrate maintaining a listening watch on the distress channel during an ongoing SAR scenario.
gold_answer: Keep the radio on Ch 16 at all times during the SAR operation, with volume set well above ambient noise and squelch at threshold. Keep DSC watch active on Ch 70. Do not transmit unless invited or providing a scheduled update. Note any instructions to shift to a working channel and comply. If required to leave the helm, hand over the watch to another SRC-qualified crew member.

Do this correctly and effective coordination of search and rescue efforts. Just be careful: ensure continuous communication and vigilance during the operation.

question: Practice transferring control of distress communication from ship to coast station once instructed.
gold_answer: On the coast station's instruction ("(vessel), THIS IS (COASTGUARD), I TAKE CONTROL, OVER") acknowledge with "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), CONTROL TRANSFERRED, OVER" and then continue to answer their questions and follow their directions. Do not initiate new priority messages unless the situation changes materially. Log the time of transfer. This releases the operator from having to lead the traffic while remaining actively involved.

question: Demonstrate repeating essential information (position, persons on board) clearly when requested by MRCC.
gold_answer: On MRCC's request, respond promptly and slowly: "THIS IS (vessel), MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO DEGREES ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE MINUTES NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DEGREES FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE MINUTES WEST, POB FIVE, INCLUDING ONE INJURED, I SAY AGAIN, POSITION FIVE ZERO ... , POB FIVE, OVER." Use digit-by-digit pronunciation, decimal instead of point, and I SAY AGAIN to guarantee the copy.

question: Show how to brief crew on their roles during simulated distress communication.
gold_answer: Assign roles clearly before the simulation: one person on the radio (MAYDAY delivery, MRCC dialogue), one on the DSC/GPS confirming position, one on lookout and preparing safety equipment (liferaft, EPIRB, grab bag), one in charge of casualty if any. Rehearse the sequence with the MAYDAY card and confirm each role knows their trigger. Debrief after the drill to identify improvements.
expected_points: assign radio, DSC/GPS, lookout, casualty roles
rehearse the sequence with a MAYDAY card

Do this correctly and crew members will be prepared for distress situations and know their responsibilities. Just be careful: ensure all crew members are aware of their roles to prevent confusion during an actual emergency.

question: Demonstrate switching from the initial distress channel to a working channel when directed by MRCC.
gold_answer: On MRCC's instruction ("(vessel), THIS IS (COASTGUARD), CHANGE TO CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER"), acknowledge ("(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), GOING TO CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER") and switch. On the new channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER." MRCC then continues coordination there, freeing Ch 16 for further distress traffic if needed.

question: Show how to relay a distress call from another vessel that you hear weakly, according to proper format.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 transmit: "MAYDAY RELAY, MAYDAY RELAY, MAYDAY RELAY, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (own vessel x3), MMSI (…), FOLLOWING RECEIVED FROM (distress vessel name), POSITION (as heard), NATURE OF DISTRESS (as heard), TIME OF ORIGINAL CALL (UTC), OVER." Follow up any coast station acknowledgement with additional detail as it becomes available.

question: Demonstrate giving periodic updates on the vessel's situation during an ongoing distress.
gold_answer: Every 5–10 minutes (or when the situation changes materially), transmit an update: "MAYDAY, THIS IS (vessel), UPDATE — (vessel is now taking water in the forecabin), (crew members are wearing life jackets), (life raft ready to launch), (POB still five), OVER." Keep updates factual and short so MRCC can maintain accurate situational awareness.
expected_points: update every 5–10 minutes or on material change

Do this correctly and MRCC is informed of the vessel's ongoing distress and can take appropriate actions. Just be careful: do not lose contact with MRCC as it may affect rescue efforts.

question: Show how to terminate distress communications when instructed by MRCC and return to routine watch.
gold_answer: MRCC will announce: "ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (COASTGUARD), SEELONCE FEENEE, TIME (UTC), OUT." Acknowledge on request, then resume routine listening watch on Ch 16 and DSC on Ch 70. Log the time and reason for termination, the assisting units involved, and any lessons learned. Consider a short crew debrief once the situation is safe.

Do this correctly and the vessel will remain safe while awaiting further instructions from MRCC. Just be careful: do not transmit any signals or sounds that could be mistaken for distress signals unless in genuine distress.

question: Demonstrate the correct use of the radio in a simulated abandon-ship scenario.
gold_answer: Before abandoning, send a DSC distress alert with nature ABANDONING SHIP and a full voice MAYDAY on Ch 16 stating the intention and time to abandon. Take a handheld VHF (and EPIRB, PLB, SART if available) into the liferaft. Once in the raft, keep the handheld VHF dry and switched off until you have reason to transmit — battery life is precious. Use the handheld to talk to SAR units on Ch 16 during approach.

answer: First, switch on the radio; Then, set to Channel 16; Next, transmit 'Mayday, Mayday, Mayday'; After that, state your vessel name three times; Finally, provide your position clearly; Then, declare the nature of distress; Then, count down from ten at two-minute intervals; Then, transmit 'All stations, this is...'. Do this correctly and other vessels and rescue services will be alerted to the distress situation. Just be careful: ensure the radio is operational before initiating distress calls.

question: Show how to coordinate with another assisting vessel via VHF during the SAR exercise.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 (or the working channel assigned by MRCC), exchange positions, courses, speeds and intended actions with the other assisting vessel using SMCP structure. Agree on the search pattern (parallel, expanding square) and the reporting interval. Keep messages brief and coordinated with MRCC's overall picture — often one of the vessels is designated as On-Scene Coordinator (OSC).
expected_points: agree search pattern and reporting interval

Do this correctly and both vessels confirmed their intentions and agreed on the course alteration. Just be careful: maintain a safe distance to avoid collision.

question: Demonstrate handling of simultaneous incoming DSC distress alerts and selecting the one to respond to under guidance.
gold_answer: If two DSC distress alerts arrive at once (simulator scenario), silence both alarms, list them by MMSI and position, and consult the coast station on Ch 16 for direction. MRCC will typically instruct which vessel to prioritise based on immediacy of danger, proximity of your vessel and available SAR units. Do not attempt to respond to both simultaneously.

Do this correctly and the selected distress alert is acknowledged and the operator can proceed with further actions. Just be careful: do not press the DISTRESS key without selecting a specific station to avoid unnecessary alerts.

question: Show how to conduct a short debrief explaining what went well and what could be improved in the distress exercise.
gold_answer: After the exercise gather the crew, review the sequence of events on the log, and structure the debrief around three questions: what worked (correct pro-words, quick DSC action, clear MRCC contact); what did not (slow position readouts, missed I SAY AGAIN, forgotten POB); what to change next time (rehearse MAYDAY card, pre-programme MRCC MMSI, improve GPS accuracy). question: On a simulator, perform a PAN PAN voice call for loss of engine power in a busy fairway.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (lat/long), URGENCY: TOTAL LOSS OF ENGINE POWER IN CENTRAL FAIRWAY, DRIFTING WITH TIDAL SET TO NORTH-EAST AT 2 KNOTS, POB FOUR, VESSEL SAILING VESSEL 12 METRES, REQUEST TUG ASSISTANCE, OVER." Do this correctly and other vessels and stations will be alerted to the emergency situation. Just be careful: ensure the distress call is only used in genuine emergencies.

question: Demonstrate how to update the coastguard when a tug has arrived to assist after a PAN PAN call.
gold_answer: On the assigned working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), UPDATE — TUG (name) IS ALONGSIDE AT POSITION (…), TOW COMMENCING TO (destination), URGENCY TRAFFIC ENDS AT MY NEXT TRANSMISSION, THIS IS (vessel), OVER." Just be careful: if the vessel is unable to make way, it may require immediate assistance.

question: Show how to downgrade a situation from PAN PAN to routine once the immediate danger has passed.
gold_answer: On the working channel used with MRCC: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), SITUATION UNDER CONTROL, URGENCY TRAFFIC ENDS, PATIENT RECOVERED, NO ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, THANK YOU, OUT." question: Demonstrate how to call a coast station to ask whether an urgency message is appropriate before transmitting.
gold_answer: If unsure whether the situation warrants PAN PAN, call the coastguard first on their working channel (e.g. Ch 67 in the UK): "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), ROUTINE, REQUEST ADVICE, OVER." question: Perform a simulated urgency call for loss of steering gear in open water.

Follow the MRCC's directions.

Do this correctly and successful transmission of the urgency call and acknowledgment from the coast station. Just be careful: ensure to follow proper procedures for distress and urgency calls.

question: Demonstrate providing clear and calm updates about the vessel's drift and conditions during the urgency scenario.
gold_answer: Every few minutes on the assigned channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), UPDATE — POSITION (…), DRIFT NOW EAST-NORTH-EAST AT 1.5 KNOTS, WIND 15 KNOTS, DISTANCE TO COAST FIVE MILES AND CLOSING, OVER." Keep the tone calm and factual. If a change requires escalation to MAYDAY (e.g. imminent grounding), announce it clearly.

question: Show how to respond as a nearby vessel when hearing a PAN PAN call that you are well-placed to assist.
gold_answer: After the coast station has responded (or if there is no response after a reasonable interval), transmit: "(distress vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), RECEIVED PAN PAN, MY POSITION (…), ETA TO YOUR POSITION (…), READY TO ASSIST, OVER." question: Demonstrate how to request towing assistance via a PAN PAN call without overstating the danger.
gold_answer: Deliver the PAN PAN using factual language: state the failure (engine, steering, etc.), the current drift and sea room, and clearly state "REQUEST TOW" as the assistance needed. Do this correctly and the coastguard or other vessels will be alerted to your situation and may offer assistance. Just be careful: do not exaggerate the danger; it should be clear that assistance is needed but not overstated.

question: Show how to log details of an urgency communication and subsequent developments.
gold_answer: Record in the log: UTC time of PAN PAN, channel used, coast station MMSI/name, position, nature of urgency, POB, assistance requested, MRCC instructions received, any assisting vessels or tugs (names / MMSIs), time when situation was downgraded and reason. answer: First, log the details of the urgency communication; Then, acknowledge further developments with 'PAN-PAN' or 'SECURITE'; Next, update the log as new information becomes available. Do this correctly and the log provides a comprehensive record of the urgency situation and its resolution. Just be careful: ensure all communications are logged promptly to maintain accountability.

question: Perform a scenario where a minor medical issue slowly escalates and you decide when to issue PAN PAN.
gold_answer: Track vital signs and behaviour; if the crew member's condition deteriorates (loss of consciousness, chest pain, severe bleeding), that is the moment to escalate. If deterioration continues towards a life-threatening state, further escalate to MAYDAY.

Two forms guard against a single-source error.

Do this correctly and the other vessel is informed of the current situation and can provide appropriate assistance. Just be careful: ensure all information is accurate to avoid confusion during the distress call.

question: Show how to coordinate with harbour control regarding an urgency situation inside a port area.

Keep the port control channel priority, comply with instructions and log all exchanges.

question: Demonstrate switching between distress and urgency channels if directed by MRCC.
gold_answer: MRCC may instruct: "(vessel), THIS IS (COASTGUARD), CHANGE TO CHANNEL SIX SEVEN FOR CONTINUED URGENCY TRAFFIC, OVER." question: Perform a role-play where you must explain to crew why PAN PAN, not MAYDAY, is being used.

question: Show how to request an updated weather forecast from a coast station during an urgency scenario.

question: Demonstrate how to cancel an urgency condition once a tow or rescue vessel has taken control.

answer: First, wait 5 minutes after receiving a SECURITÉ broadcast; Then, if no further information is received, repeat the broadcast; Next, contact the coast station that transmitted the SECURITÉ message. Do this correctly and mariners receive timely updates on weather conditions. Just be careful: do not transmit false SECURITÉ messages.

question: Demonstrate how to log a received safety broadcast that affects your planned route.
gold_answer: In the log record: UTC time received, channel, coast station identity, brief summary of the hazard or warning (type, position, effect on navigation), and the action taken (course change, extra watch, reduction in sail). Plot the hazard on the chart if practical. Note any subsequent updates or cancellations. This gives an evidential trail if the hazard later becomes an incident.
expected_points: plot on chart and note updates
answer: First, log the safety broadcast in the ship’s log; Then, note the time and channel of the broadcast; Next, plot the reported position on the chart; After that, join the reported position with your current position; Finally, calculate a safe distance for the next reporting point; Then, adjust the passage plan accordingly. Do this correctly and improved situational awareness regarding navigational hazards. Just be careful: ensure to maintain a safe distance from reported hazards.

question: Perform a safety call to inform nearby traffic about your restricted manoeuvrability during towing operations.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), COURSE ZERO NINE ZERO, SPEED THREE KNOTS, VESSEL RESTRICTED IN ABILITY TO MANOEUVRE DUE TO TOWING OPERATIONS, TOWING (name of towed vessel) ASTERN, LENGTH OF TOW (…) METRES, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, OUT." Repeat every 30 minutes while the operation continues.
expected_points: state RESTRICTED IN ABILITY TO MANOEUVRE
identify towed vessel and tow length
advise vessels to keep clear; repeat every 30 min
answer: First, perform a safety call on Channel 16; Then, broadcast a safety message on Channel 72. Do this correctly and nearby vessels are informed of the towing operation and advised to keep clear. Just be careful: maintain a safe distance from the vessel engaged in towing operations.

question: Show how to respond to a SECURITÉ message requesting vessels to keep clear of a SAR area.
gold_answer: Note the position and extent of the SAR area, plot it on the chart, and adjust the passage plan to keep well clear (typically at least 2 nm unless the message states otherwise). Reduce speed and post an extra lookout. If your route inevitably passes near the area, call the coastguard on their working channel to confirm safe transit or an alternative route. Log the message and the action taken.
expected_points: note position and extent of SAR area
plot on chart, adjust passage plan
reduce speed and post extra lookout
call coastguard if route passes near
answer: First, acknowledge the SECURITÉ message; Then, comply with the request to keep clear of the area; Next, monitor Channel 16 and report any sightings. Do this correctly and increased safety for search and rescue operations. Just be careful: vessels must keep clear of the specified area.

question: Demonstrate how to broadcast a safety message about a drifting object dangerous to navigation.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: LARGE DRIFTING TIMBER OBSERVED IN POSITION (lat/long) AT (time UTC), APPROXIMATELY FIFTEEN METRES LONG, HALF-SUBMERGED, DRIFTING NORTH-EAST, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, OUT." Follow up with coastguard on a working channel for rebroadcast and logging.
expected_points: advise keep clear; follow up with coastguard
answer: First, broadcast a safety message on Channel 16; Then, wait 5 minutes; Next, broadcast the safety message again on Channel 16; After that, wait 5 minutes; Finally, broadcast the safety message once more on Channel 16. Do this correctly and mariners are informed of the danger posed by the drifting object. Just be careful: the object is dangerous to navigation.

question: Perform a scenario where you transmit a safety message advising of reduced visibility in a narrow channel.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: FOG IN (channel name), VISIBILITY LESS THAN TWO HUNDRED METRES, WIND CALM, VESSELS ADVISED PROCEED WITH CAUTION AND MAINTAIN LISTENING WATCH ON CHANNEL ONE SIX, OUT." Update every 30 minutes or when conditions change materially.
expected_points: update every 30 min or on change
answer: First, transmit a safety message; Then, state the position and extent of the area with reduced visibility; Next, specify the duration of the reduced visibility. Do this correctly and mariners are informed about the reduced visibility conditions and can adjust their navigation accordingly. Just be careful: navigation should be conducted with caution due to reduced visibility.

question: Show how to receive and acknowledge MSI (Maritime Safety Information) relevant to your voyage.
gold_answer: Once the coastguard's SÉCURITÉ announcement on Ch 16 directs listeners to the MSI working channel, switch to that channel and listen to the full text — no acknowledgement is expected during the broadcast. Log the relevant portions (gale warning, hazard position, NAVTEX message ID) and cross-check on the chart. If a specific portion was missed, request repetition on the working channel afterwards.
expected_points: listen to SÉCURITÉ announcement on Ch 16
log relevant portions and cross-check on chart
answer: First, listen on 2182 kHz MF; Then, set your VHF DSC to receive GMDSS MSI; Next, check with the nearest HMCG MRCC or SSB for latest warnings. Do this correctly and you will receive timely Maritime Safety Information (MSI) relevant to your voyage. Just be careful: ensure you have access to a means of receiving MSI.

question: Demonstrate how to switch channels when instructed to listen to a scheduled safety broadcast.
gold_answer: When the coastguard announces on Ch 16: "...ALL STATIONS SHIFT TO CHANNEL SIX TWO, SIX THREE OR SIX FOUR, OVER.", switch to the announced channel using knob, up/down or keypad entry. Confirm the display shows the new number. Listen to the broadcast, log key content and return to Ch 16 watch afterwards. Some sets do this automatically via NAVTEX-style scheduling.
answer: First, switch to the appropriate channel; Then, listen for 5 minutes; Next, return to the working channel. Do this correctly and the mariner will receive important safety information during the scheduled broadcast.

question: Perform a SECURITÉ message regarding a malfunctioning navigation light on your own vessel that may confuse others.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), COURSE (…), SPEED (…), SAFETY INFORMATION: MY STARBOARD NAVIGATION LIGHT NOT WORKING, TEMPORARY REPLACEMENT (torch/emergency light) IN USE, REQUEST VESSELS APPROACHING FROM MY STARBOARD SIDE MAINTAIN EXTRA CAUTION, VESSEL WILL PROCEED TO NEAREST HARBOUR, OUT." Repeat if the situation persists.
expected_points: request extra caution from other vessels
answer: First, transmit a SECURITÉ safety message; Then, provide your position, the nature of your problem, and your intentions. Do this correctly and other vessels are informed of the potential hazard and can take appropriate action to avoid collision. Just be careful: ensure the message is transmitted on Channel 16 only when there is no other means of contacting coast stations or rescue authorities.

question: Show how to coordinate with harbour control when reporting a small oil spill seen near the entrance.
gold_answer: On port control channel (e.g. Ch 12): "(PORT) HARBOUR CONTROL, THIS IS (vessel), REPORTING AN OIL SLICK NEAR THE HARBOUR ENTRANCE, POSITION (…), APPROXIMATELY (size) SQUARE METRES, DRIFTING (direction), NO SOURCE VESSEL IN SIGHT, OVER." Provide any additional info (colour, sheen, smell). Harbour control will task pollution response and may broadcast a warning to other vessels.
expected_points: call port control on its channel
report position and size of slick
follow up as tasked by harbour control
answer: First, report position of the spill; Then, indicate size of the spill; Next, specify type of oil; After that, state visibility; Finally, mention wind direction and force; Then, indicate sea conditions; Then, inform about tide levels; Then, state if the spill is increasing or decreasing; Then, ask if harbour control can send a pollution clearance team; Then, request if harbour control can send a tug for assistance. Do this correctly and effective communication of the spill details to relevant authorities. Just be careful: ensure safety while assessing the spill situation.

question: Demonstrate how to phrase a safety message without causing undue alarm.
gold_answer: Use factual language and standard SMCP structure. State the hazard, position, effect on navigation and advised action. Avoid words like "emergency", "disaster" or subjective phrases such as "very dangerous" — the SÉCURITÉ prefix already signals priority. Example: "...NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: DRIFTING CONTAINER IN POSITION (…), APPROXIMATELY 6 METRES LONG, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR..." is calm and specific.
answer: First, address 'All stations' at the start of the safety message; Then, use 'This is ...', followed by the name of your vessel and your MMSI; Next, state 'Safety, Safety, Safety'; After that, provide the safety message; Finally, end with 'Out'. Do this correctly and other vessels will receive the safety information without unnecessary alarm. Just be careful: ensure the safety message is clear and does not cause undue alarm.

question: Perform role-play where you repeat a safety message to another vessel that missed it.
gold_answer: On the vessel's working channel (or if urgent, on Ch 16): "(vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), RELAY OF SAFETY MESSAGE — NAVIGATIONAL WARNING RECEIVED FROM COASTGUARD AT (time UTC): DRIFTING CONTAINER IN POSITION (…), VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, OVER." Give the other vessel time to acknowledge and offer to repeat if needed. Log the relay.
expected_points: include time and content of the original
answer: First, repeat the safety message; Then, state the name of the vessel that missed the message; Next, say 'over'. Do this correctly and the other vessel is informed of the safety message. Just be careful: ensure the other vessel receives the safety information.

question: Show how to adjust radio procedures depending on whether you are originating or merely relaying safety information.
gold_answer: When originating, use the SÉCURITÉ prefix on Ch 16 and provide direct observation data (what you saw, when, where). When relaying an existing safety message from another station, identify the original source (e.g. "RECEIVED FROM COASTGUARD AT (time)"), so the recipient knows the information is second-hand. The distinction affects accountability and the recipient's assessment of currency.
expected_points: originating: SÉCURITÉ prefix with direct observation
relaying: identify original source and time
state the message content verbatim if possible
answer: First, adjust procedures according to your position; Then, ensure clear communication of safety information. Do this correctly and improved clarity in safety communications.

question: Demonstrate good logging practices for safety messages, including source, time, and content summary.
gold_answer: Log entries should include: UTC time received or transmitted, channel, source (coastguard, other vessel or own observation), message category (navigational warning, weather warning, SAR area, MSI), content summary (position, hazard type, effect), and action taken by the vessel (course change, extra watch, relay). Keep entries factual and chronological to support subsequent audits or coastguard follow-up.
answer: First, log all safety messages; Then, indicate if the message is from a foreign coast station or not; Next, note the language of the message; After that, record the time when the message was received; Finally, summarize the content of the safety message. Do this correctly and improved safety awareness among crew members regarding current maritime safety information. Just be careful: ensure to log all safety messages promptly to avoid missing critical information.

question: Perform a simulated response where you divert the vessel's route based on a received safety broadcast.
gold_answer: After receiving the SÉCURITÉ (e.g. drifting container in your planned route), plot the hazard on the chart, calculate a safe passing distance (typically ≥ 2 nm), plan the new course and communicate the plan to the crew. If required, notify VTS or harbour control of the diversion: "(VTS), THIS IS (vessel), IN VIEW OF HAZARD REPORTED AT (time), DIVERTING NORTHWARD TO PASS AT LATITUDE (…), OVER." Log the change.
expected_points: plot hazard and plan safe passing distance (≥ 2 nm)
brief the crew on the new plan
answer: First, acknowledge the safety announcement; Then, inform passengers and crew of the situation; Next, prepare for possible evacuation; After that, maintain communication with rescue authorities; Finally, divert the vessel's course to avoid the danger area. Do this correctly and increased awareness of the danger area and potential evacuation readiness. Just be careful: danger area ahead, navigate with caution.

question: Show how to query a coast station for clarification about a hazard mentioned in a previous safety broadcast.
gold_answer: On the coast station's working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REGARDING NAVIGATIONAL WARNING BROADCAST AT (time UTC), REQUEST CLARIFICATION OF (specific element, e.g. exact position, duration of warning), OVER." The coast station will provide the requested detail. Log the response and update the passage plan accordingly.
expected_points: call on coast station's working channel
reference the original broadcast by time
answer: First, acknowledge the safety announcement; Then, request immediate information from the coast station; Next, state that further information will be broadcast. Do this correctly and the Auto Pilot will inform all stations about the hazard and request immediate information from the coast station. Just be careful: do not navigate in areas with hazards until further notice.

question: Demonstrate how to advise nearby vessels of your participation in clearance work (e.g., debris removal) via SECURITÉ.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), SAFETY INFORMATION: CONDUCTING DEBRIS REMOVAL OPERATION IN AREA (…), ESTIMATED DURATION (…), VESSEL RESTRICTED IN ABILITY TO MANOEUVRE, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR OF THE AREA, OUT." Repeat every 30 minutes or when conditions change. Coordinate with harbour control if inside a port area.
expected_points: state RESTRICTED IN ABILITY TO MANOEUVRE
coordinate with harbour control if in port
answer: First, advise nearby vessels on the way ahead; Then, inform about the need for vessels to keep clear; Next, advise to proceed with caution. Do this correctly and nearby vessels are informed of the situation and advised to keep clear. Just be careful: vessels must keep clear of the area.

question: Perform a brief verbal debrief on how safety communications reduce environmental and collision risks.
gold_answer: Debrief: "SÉCURITÉ broadcasts alert every vessel in range to hazards — drifting containers, oil slicks, narrow-channel obstructions, weather deterioration — giving them time to alter course, reduce speed or reroute before an incident occurs. Over time this proactive dissemination measurably reduces collisions, groundings and pollution incidents, and supports pollution response by triggering shore action quickly."
expected_points: time to alter course or reduce speed
answer: First, make safety communications; Then, ensure navigational safety. Do this correctly and reduced risk of collisions and environmental pollution. Just be careful: safety communications are crucial for navigational safety.

question: Make a routine call to a marina to request a berth, providing all relevant vessel details.
gold_answer: On the marina's published channel (e.g. Ch 80 in the UK): "(Marina), (Marina), (Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), OVER." On reply: "(Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), TWELVE METRES LOA, TWO METRES DRAUGHT, MONOHULL SAILING YACHT, ETA ONE SIX ZERO ZERO UTC, REQUEST OVERNIGHT BERTH, POB THREE, OVER." Confirm assigned berth: "ROGER, BERTH C SEVEN, ARRIVING AT ONE SIX ZERO ZERO UTC, THANK YOU, OUT."
expected_points: call marina on published channel (e.g. Ch 80)
answer: First, make a routine call to the marina; Then, provide your MMSI and position; Next, state your ETA at the junction / fairway; After that, indicate your anchor watch and engine status; Finally, confirm your ability to receive pilot or tugs. Do this correctly and the marina will be informed of your arrival and can prepare accordingly. Just be careful: ensure you have the correct information for the marina to avoid confusion.

question: Demonstrate a routine call to a fuel dock to arrange refuelling on arrival.
gold_answer: "(Fuel dock), THIS IS (Vessel), ETA ONE FIVE MINUTES, REQUEST ONE FIVE ZERO LITRES DIESEL, WATER TOP-UP, STARBOARD SIDE ALONGSIDE, OVER." On confirmation: "THIS IS (Vessel), ROGER, WILL CALL TWO MINUTES OUT, OUT." Two minutes before arrival: "(Fuel dock), THIS IS (Vessel), TWO MINUTES OUT, OVER." Keep messages short and structured.
answer: First, make a routine call to the fuel dock; Then, confirm receipt of the fuel report; Next, acknowledge the fuel transfer start time. Do this correctly and successful confirmation of fuel arrangements.

question: Perform a ship-to-ship routine call to coordinate a passing arrangement in a narrow channel.
gold_answer: On Ch 13 (bridge-to-bridge) or Ch 16 if 13 unavailable: "(target vessel), (target vessel), (target vessel), THIS IS (own vessel) x3, OVER." On reply propose channel: "REQUEST SWITCH TO CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." On the working channel, use SMCP: "(target), THIS IS (own vessel), INTENTION: I INTEND TO OVERTAKE YOU ON YOUR STARBOARD SIDE, SPEED (…) KNOTS, OVER." Await confirmation and log the exchange.
expected_points: initial contact on Ch 13 (bridge-to-bridge) or Ch 16
answer: First, initiate a ship-to-ship routine call on Channel 16; Then, request to repeat the message on the working channel; Next, confirm receipt of the answer and state that the channel is changed. Do this correctly and both vessels agreed on the passing arrangement and confirmed the change of channel.

question: Show how to move from channel 16 to a working channel when instructed during a routine call.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 the other station may say: "...REQUEST SWITCH TO CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." Reply: "(other station), THIS IS (own vessel), GOING TO CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." Switch, then re-establish contact: "(other station), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." Conduct the conversation and close with OUT, returning both stations to Ch 16 watch.
expected_points: close with OUT and return to Ch 16 watch
answer: First, switch to the working channel; Then, repeat the name and call sign. Do this correctly and both parties confirm their understanding of the communication.

question: Demonstrate a call to harbour control requesting permission to enter and berth.
gold_answer: On port control channel (e.g. Ch 12): "(PORT NAME) HARBOUR, THIS IS (vessel) x3, OVER." On reply: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (vessel), SAILING YACHT, TWELVE METRES LOA, TWO METRES DRAUGHT, POSITION TWO MILES SOUTH OF ENTRANCE, ETA ONE TWO ZERO ZERO UTC, REQUEST PERMISSION TO ENTER AND BERTH IN VISITOR AREA, OVER." Wait for the entry instruction and readback the assigned berth or holding position.
expected_points: call harbour control on its channel
answer: First, call harbour control; Then, request permission to enter and berth; Next, confirm receipt of permission and proceed to anchorage. Do this correctly and the vessel receives permission to enter and berth safely.

question: Perform a routine call to a yacht club to confirm race start times and instructions.
gold_answer: On the club's working channel (per Sailing Instructions, e.g. Ch 72): "(Club), THIS IS (Vessel), CONFIRMING START TIME FOR (class), OVER." On reply: "(Club), THIS IS (Vessel), UNDERSTOOD START TIME ONE THREE ZERO ZERO UTC, CLASS FLAG (colour/description), THANK YOU, OUT." Log the start time and class flag for the crew brief.
expected_points: use club's working channel per SI
readback start time and class flag
answer: First, perform a routine call to the yacht club; Then, wait for a response from the yacht club; Next, acknowledge the yacht club's response and confirm monitoring VHF Channel 72. Do this correctly and the Auto Pilot confirms the race start time and location. Just be careful: ensure to monitor VHF Channel 72 for further instructions.

question: Show how to conduct a brief radio check with a known station without misusing distress channels.
gold_answer: On a working channel (e.g. Ch 9 or the marina's working channel): "(Station), THIS IS (Vessel), RADIO CHECK, OVER." On reply: "(Vessel), THIS IS (Station), READ YOU LOUD AND CLEAR, OVER." Reply: "THIS IS (Vessel), THANK YOU, OUT." Do not test on Ch 16. If a formal signal report is provided, note it in the log.
answer: First, use Channel 9 for radio checks; Then, call the other station's name twice, identify yourself, and say 'over'; Next, state 'radio check' or 'ready for you' and say 'over'; After that, wait for their radio check reply and say 'over'; Finally, confirm receipt of their signal strength and say 'over'. Do this correctly and both stations confirm their ability to communicate on the designated channel. Just be careful: do not use emergency or working channels for routine checks.

question: Demonstrate how to manage a language barrier by speaking slowly and using simple vocabulary.
gold_answer: Slow down slightly, use short SMCP phrases, avoid idioms and slang, spell difficult names phonetically, and use digit-by-digit for numbers. Break complex requests into single-idea transmissions and use readbacks: "THIS IS (vessel), I UNDERSTAND BERTH C SEVEN, I SAY AGAIN, BERTH C SEVEN, CORRECT? OVER." If misunderstanding persists, request a shift to English-speaking staff or the coastguard, who typically has English fluency.
answer: First, speak slowly; Then, use simple vocabulary; Next, repeat instructions. Do this correctly and improved communication despite language barriers.

question: Perform a routine call to a bridge operator to request an opening at a specific time.
gold_answer: On the bridge's dedicated channel: "(Bridge name), THIS IS (Vessel) x3, OVER." On reply: "(Bridge), THIS IS (Vessel), SAILING YACHT, MAST HEIGHT (…) METRES, POSITION (…), REQUEST OPENING AT ONE FOUR THREE ZERO UTC, OVER." On confirmation readback: "THIS IS (Vessel), OPENING CONFIRMED FOR ONE FOUR THREE ZERO UTC, WILL HOLD SOUTH OF BRIDGE, THANK YOU, OUT."
answer: First, perform a routine call; Then, wait for the bridge operator to respond; Next, ask when the next opening will be; After that, confirm the exact time of the next opening and note it down; Finally, say 'Thank you' and end the call. Do this correctly and the vessel receives confirmation of the next opening time.

question: Show how to close the conversation correctly with the other station using appropriate pro-words.
gold_answer: After the substantive exchange is complete: "(other station), THIS IS (own vessel), STANDING BY ON CHANNEL (channel), OUT." Or if returning to normal watch: "...RETURNING TO CHANNEL ONE-SIX, THIS IS (own vessel), OUT." This signals no reply expected, states which channel you now monitor, and confirms your vessel identity. Log the time and outcome.
expected_points: state which channel you now monitor
answer: First, say 'Over'; Then, say 'Out'. Do this correctly and clear communication of the end of a conversation.

question: Demonstrate calling a nearby yacht to coordinate rafting alongside at anchor.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: 3-3 identification, shift to an intership channel (e.g. Ch 72). On the working channel: "(other yacht), THIS IS (own vessel), REQUEST PERMISSION TO RAFT ALONGSIDE, WE ARE APPROACHING FROM NORTH-WEST, WILL COME PORT SIDE ALONGSIDE YOUR STARBOARD, POB (…), OVER." Await confirmation and coordinate approach and fender arrangement. Close with OUT.
expected_points: Ch 16 initial contact, shift to Ch 72
coordinate fenders and close with OUT
answer: First, call the yacht 'Breeze' on Channel 16; Then, confirm the call is for the correct vessel; Next, state your position and intention to raft alongside; After that, request their confirmation to proceed with the plan; Finally, acknowledge their confirmation and prepare to adjust course. Do this correctly and both vessels agreed to raft alongside safely. Just be careful: ensure the yacht is anchored before proceeding with the plan.

question: Perform a role-play where a mis-heard instruction is clarified using "SAY AGAIN" and phonetic spelling.
gold_answer: If the harbour master says "BERTH BAKER SEVEN" and it is unclear: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel), SAY AGAIN THE BERTH DESIGNATION, OVER." Harbour master responds: "THIS IS (HARBOUR), BERTH BAKER SEVEN, I SPELL BRAVO-ALFA-KILO-ECHO-ROMEO, SEVEN, OVER." Readback: "THIS IS (Vessel), BERTH BAKER SEVEN, I SPELL BRAVO-ALFA-KILO-ECHO-ROMEO, SEVEN, OVER." Harbour master confirms.
expected_points: use SAY AGAIN to request repetition
harbour master uses I SPELL with phonetic
answer: First, acknowledge the request to repeat the instruction; Then, spell out the word 'anchor' using phonetic alphabet; Next, confirm understanding of the new instruction. Do this correctly and both parties confirm the corrected instruction regarding the anchoring position.

question: Show how to refuse an unsafe request from another vessel politely over VHF.
gold_answer: Use standard SMCP: "(other vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), NEGATIVE — I AM UNABLE TO (specific action) DUE TO (reason, e.g. draught limitations, sea state), REGRET NO ASSISTANCE POSSIBLE, OVER." Keep the refusal factual and brief, without judgement. If safety is genuinely at risk (e.g. request would put your vessel in danger), state that clearly so MRCC understands.
answer: First, respond to the other vessel's call; Then, state that you will not comply with their request; Next, provide a reason for your decision; After that, suggest a safe alternative if possible. Do this correctly and both vessels maintain safety and compliance with navigation rules. Just be careful: do not comply with requests that could endanger lives or property.

question: Demonstrate the use of low power for local routine communications in a marina.
gold_answer: Press H/L to select LOW (1 W) before transmitting inside a marina or at short range. Confirm the display shows LO. Make the call as normal — a marina berthing exchange, a courtesy call to another yacht. Return to high power (25 W) once leaving the marina area or before making a coast station or distress call. Low power reduces both interference and battery drain.
expected_points: press H/L to select LOW (1 W)
use in marina or short range
return to high (25 W) offshore or for distress
answer: First, switch to Channel 06; Then, set power to low. Do this correctly and reduced interference with other vessels. Just be careful: ensure to switch back to the working channel after use.

question: Perform a routine call to request updated depth information from harbour control.
gold_answer: On port control channel: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel), REQUEST LATEST DEPTH AT (specific area, e.g. NORTH ENTRANCE) FOR VESSEL TWO METRES DRAUGHT, OVER." Harbour control replies with the current depth (chart datum + tidal height) and any dredge or spoil information. Readback and confirm. Log the depth and time received.
answer: First, perform a routine call; Then, wait for the response from harbour control; Next, record the updated information in the log-book. Do this correctly and the pilot receives updated information regarding the channel depth.

question: Show how to handle simultaneous routine calls by instructing one caller to "STANDBY".
gold_answer: Answer each caller in turn on Ch 16 or the working channel: "(caller A), THIS IS (own vessel), STANDBY, OVER." Then answer caller B fully. Once done: "(caller A), THIS IS (own vessel), OVER." Handle in priority order (safety-related first), and if a wait exceeds a minute or two, use "STANDBY OUT" to free the channel.
expected_points: STANDBY OUT if wait exceeds 1–2 minutes
answer: First, respond to the first call; Then, inform the second caller that you are busy and will return to their call shortly; Next, respond to the second call after finishing the first. Do this correctly and both callers receive timely responses. Just be careful: do not ignore calls from multiple stations simultaneously.

question: Demonstrate logging an important routine communication (e.g., pilotage advice).
gold_answer: In the log record: UTC time, channel used, station name (e.g. Solent VTS), a factual summary of the pilotage advice (recommended course, holding position, tidal window), any instruction to switch channel, and confirmation given (readback). This creates a durable record that supports subsequent decisions and any incident review.
answer: First, log the communication; Then, indicate if recording is discontinued. Do this correctly and the communication is recorded for future reference.

question: Perform a short routine call with minimal words but full clarity, demonstrating concise communication.
gold_answer: Example: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel), TWO MINUTES OUT, LOCK ONE, PERMISSION TO ENTER, OVER." On reply: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel), ROGER, LOCK ONE, OUT." Only essential information — identity, position/timing, request — is included, and the exchange is closed cleanly. This is the SMCP ideal for routine calls.
expected_points: state single action (permission to enter Lock 1)
ROGER + station and OUT to close
answer: First, perform a short routine call; Then, initiate the call with 'Over'; Next, respond to a reply with 'Out'. Do this correctly and clear communication of operational requests or questions.

question: Show how to re-establish contact with a station after a temporary radio or power failure.
gold_answer: After power is restored, verify the radio has booted normally, GPS position and MMSI are correct, and Ch 16 (or the working channel) is set. Then call the station: "(station), THIS IS (own vessel), FOLLOWING TEMPORARY LOSS OF COMMUNICATION, NOW BACK IN CONTACT, POSITION (…), OVER." Apologise briefly, confirm any previously agreed instructions (berth, ETA), and resume the exchange.
answer: First, wait 5 minutes; Then, call the other station on Channel 16 or 2; Next, state 'This is... over'; After that, change to another working channel; Finally, say 'Out'. Do this correctly and successful re-establishment of communication with the other station.

question: Demonstrate using a handheld radio to coordinate mooring lines with crew while also communicating with harbour staff on the fixed radio.
gold_answer: Use the handheld on a low-power intership channel (e.g. Ch 72) to talk to the crew forward: "BOW LINE ON, WAITING FOR SPRING." Simultaneously the fixed radio remains on the harbour control channel for berthing instructions. Assign a crew member with SRC to monitor Ch 16 on the fixed set if you are focused on manoeuvring. Keep messages short and structured on both radios.
expected_points: handheld on intership channel (e.g. Ch 72), low power
fixed radio on harbour control channel
Ch 16 watch maintained by SRC-qualified crew
answer: First, pick up the handheld radio and hold it at chest level; Then, speak clearly into the microphone; Next, press the transmit button to send your message; After that, listen for a response from the other station; Finally, repeat your message if no response is heard after 10-15 seconds; Then, switch to the fixed radio for communication with harbour staff. Do this correctly and effective coordination of mooring operations and communication with harbour staff. Just be careful: ensure clear communication to avoid misunderstandings during critical operations.

question: Demonstrate programming the ship's MMSI into the DSC unit (or explain and show on simulator menu).
gold_answer: On the DSC menu open PROGRAM MMSI (usually inside SETUP). Enter the nine-digit MMSI issued by the national administration and confirm with ENTER. Most radios require the MMSI to be entered twice for confirmation and, once saved, lock the MMSI so it can only be changed by manufacturer reset. Verify the stored MMSI on the STATION ID screen. Never invent an MMSI or enter another vessel's.
expected_points: enter nine-digit MMSI issued by administration
answer: First, program the ship's MMSI into the DSC unit; Then, set the DSC unit to 'High Priority' for distress alerts; Next, ensure the DSC unit is always powered on. Do this correctly and the DSC unit will automatically send distress alerts with the vessel's MMSI when the button is pressed. Just be careful: ensure the DSC unit is always powered on to receive distress alerts.

question: Show how to send a DSC individual routine call to a specified MMSI and then speak on the working channel.
gold_answer: Open DSC → INDIVIDUAL CALL → ROUTINE. Enter target MMSI, select working channel (e.g. Ch 72), press SEND. On acceptance both radios auto-switch. Then: "(target vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." Proceed with substantive traffic; close with OUT and both return to Ch 16 watch afterwards.
expected_points: enter target MMSI and working channel
close with OUT and return to Ch 16
answer: First, send an individual DSC routine call; Then, wait 5 minutes; Next, send the call again; After that, wait 1 minute; Finally, speak on the working channel. Do this correctly and the call is successfully transmitted to the specified MMSI.

question: Demonstrate sending a DSC all-ships safety call (on simulator only).
gold_answer: On the simulator open DSC → ALL SHIPS → SAFETY. Confirm GPS position, select follow-up channel (typically Ch 16), and press SEND. The simulator transmits the safety alert on Ch 70 with own MMSI, position and safety category, then switches to Ch 16 for the voice SÉCURITÉ message. Follow up immediately with the voice SÉCURITÉ.
expected_points: confirm GPS position and follow-up channel
transmits on Ch 70 with safety category
answer: First, select 'All Ships' from the menu; Then, choose the appropriate safety level: 1, 2, or 3; Next, scroll down to find the message 'Safety Message'; After that, press the 'Send' key; Finally, ensure the set is tuned to Channel 70. Do this correctly and the DSC all-ships safety call is transmitted on Channel 70. Just be careful: ensure the set is tuned to Channel 70 before sending the call.

question: Show how to send a DSC urgency alert and then follow with the appropriate voice call.
gold_answer: Open DSC → ALL SHIPS → URGENCY (or INDIVIDUAL for a specific coast station). Confirm GPS position, select Ch 16 as voice follow-up channel, press SEND. The radio transmits on Ch 70 with urgency category, then auto-switches to Ch 16. Immediately transmit the voice PAN PAN with all standard elements. Log the exchange.
expected_points: confirm GPS position and follow-up channel
answer: First, press the red URG button for 5 seconds; Then, select the nature of urgency from the menu; Next, ensure MMSI is linked to your account; After that, make a voice call on channel 16 or 2182 kHz after sending the DSC urgency alert. Do this correctly and the coast station will acknowledge the DSC urgency alert and may request further details. Just be careful: do not transmit voice calls on channels 70 or 13.

question: Demonstrate reading and interpreting a received DSC distress alert on the display.
gold_answer: On alarm, silence with ALARM CANCEL and read the display: sender's MMSI, nature of distress (or UNDESIGNATED), position (lat/long), UTC time of position, and follow-up channel. Note MID (first 3 digits of MMSI) for flag state. Switch to Ch 16 and listen for the voice MAYDAY and coast station acknowledgement. Log all details.
expected_points: note MMSI, nature, position, time, channel
answer: First, read the alert details; Then, note the MMSI and position; Next, inform the appropriate coast station(s); After that, enter details in the log. Do this correctly and the distress alert is communicated effectively to relevant authorities. Just be careful: ensure to follow proper procedures to avoid miscommunication during emergencies.

question: Show how to cancel a routine DSC call before it is transmitted.
gold_answer: During the compose/preview step press ESC or CANCEL to abort. If SEND has been pressed but the radio is still in the short pre-transmission delay, press CANCEL again — many sets will still block the transmission. Once transmitted, the call cannot be recalled; if incorrect, follow up with a corrective INDIVIDUAL call to the same target using DSC or voice.
expected_points: confirm the abort on the display
answer: First, press the PTT button; Then, select 'Cancel' or 'Purge' from the menu; Next, confirm the cancellation. Do this correctly and the DSC call will not be transmitted.

question: Demonstrate how to set up and send a DSC group call to a pre-defined group MMSI.
gold_answer: Open DSC → GROUP CALL, select the pre-programmed group MMSI (nine-digit starting with a leading zero, e.g. 023201234), choose the working channel, and press SEND. All radios with that group MMSI programmed will alert simultaneously. Follow up on the working channel with the group broadcast (e.g. rendezvous point or muster instruction).
expected_points: group MMSI starts with leading zero
voice follow-up on the working channel
answer: First, select the pre-defined group MMSI from the directory; Then, choose the appropriate category (e.g., distress, safety, urgency); Next, scroll down to find the specific nature of the call; After that, set the priority level; Finally, transmit the call. Do this correctly and the DSC group call is successfully transmitted to all stations with the selected MMSI.

question: Show how to verify GPS position data on the DSC radio and update it manually if necessary.
gold_answer: Check the position display: lat/long and UTC time should be current, no NO GPS warning. If GPS is unavailable, open MANUAL POSITION, enter lat/long (with hemispheres) and UTC time, and save. Display now shows MAN or USER indicator. Update the manual position every few minutes while GPS is unavailable, so any subsequent DSC distress alert has an accurate position.
expected_points: check position display and NO GPS warning
enter lat/long with hemispheres and UTC
update every few minutes while GPS is lost
answer: First, verify GPS position data; Then, update position manually if necessary; Next, ensure MMSI is correctly programmed. Do this correctly and accurate vessel position reporting for search and rescue operations. Just be careful: incorrect MMSI programming can lead to false identity in communications.

question: Demonstrate accessing the DSC call log and reviewing stored incoming alerts.
gold_answer: Open DSC → LOG → RECEIVED (or filter by DISTRESS / URGENCY / SAFETY / ROUTINE). Scroll to individual entries and press ENTER to view: MMSI, category, UTC time, position, follow-up channel. This is useful for reviewing missed alerts or reconstructing events. Some sets separate received and transmitted logs; check both.
expected_points: view MMSI, category, time, position, channel
check both received and transmitted logs
answer: First, press the 'CALL LOG' key; Then, scroll through the log entries; Next, find an incoming alert and press 'ENTER'; After that, read the details of the alert. Do this correctly and you can review all DSC calls and alerts made to or from your radio.

question: Show how to respond to a DSC routine call directed at your vessel.
gold_answer: When the DSC alerts, note the caller's MMSI and proposed channel on the display. Press ACCEPT / ACK — the radio switches automatically to the proposed channel. Reply by voice: "(caller), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL (…), OVER." Proceed with the substantive exchange. If the channel is unsuitable, press REJECT and call the caller manually with an alternative.
expected_points: read caller MMSI and proposed channel
REJECT and manual call if channel unsuitable
answer: First, listen on channel 6 for 5 minutes; Then, if no DSC acknowledgement is received, call again after 5 minutes; Next, if still no response, call a third time after another 5 minutes; After that, switch to voice on channel 16 and call the coast station. Do this correctly and the coast station will be contacted and able to assist with the emergency. Just be careful: ensure to listen on the correct channels to avoid missing important communications.

question: Demonstrate the correct sequence after receiving a DSC distress alert (voice follow-up, logging, standby).
gold_answer: 1. Silence alarm; note MMSI, nature, position, time. 2. Switch to Ch 16 (usually automatic). 3. Wait ~5 minutes in Sea Area A1 for the coast station to acknowledge — do not talk over. 4. If no coast station response and you can help, transmit acknowledgement and offer of assistance on Ch 16. 5. Log everything: time, MMSI, nature, position, coast station response, actions taken. Maintain listening watch until MRCC clears the incident.
expected_points: wait ~5 min for coast station in Sea Area A1
offer assistance only if no coast station responds
answer: First, acknowledge the DSC alert; Then, transmit the voice distress alert; Next, copy the distress message in the log; After that, stand by specified stations for instructions. Do this correctly and the distress alert is communicated effectively to all relevant parties. Just be careful: ensure all communications are logged for accountability.

question: Show how to mute and un-mute DSC alarms while still maintaining awareness.
gold_answer: When an alarm sounds, press ALARM CANCEL or SILENCE to mute the tone for the current alert while keeping the DSC watch active on Ch 70. Address the alert (read details, take action), then confirm the alarm system is fully re-enabled. Do not globally disable DSC alarms — this defeats the purpose of GMDSS watchkeeping.
expected_points: ALARM CANCEL / SILENCE for current alert
answer: First, press the Mute key; Then, wait five minutes; Next, check the DSC alarm indicator light; After that, un-mute by pressing the Mute key again. Do this correctly and DSC alarms are silenced for five minutes to prevent continuous alerts. Just be careful: DSC alarms will sound continuously until muted or acknowledged.

question: Demonstrate storing a new MMSI in the DSC directory for frequent contacts.
gold_answer: Open DSC → DIRECTORY → NEW ENTRY. Enter the MMSI (verify with the vessel's owner or from the MMSI database), and give it a memorable label (e.g. "COASTGUARD SOLENT" or "FLOTILLA LEAD"). Save. Future INDIVIDUAL or GROUP calls can then be launched by selecting the name rather than typing the MMSI, reducing errors.
expected_points: future calls select by name to reduce errors
answer: First, store the new MMSI in the DSC directory; Then, program the MMSI into the DSC's memory. Do this correctly and the DSC can automatically send distress alerts or call specific stations using the stored MMSI.

question: Show how to modify or delete an incorrect MMSI entry from the directory.
gold_answer: Open DSC → DIRECTORY, select the entry to modify, press EDIT, change the MMSI or label, and save. To delete, select the entry and choose DELETE (some sets require confirmation). Verify the change and test with an INDIVIDUAL call to the corrected MMSI where practical. Keep the directory up to date so calls do not go to the wrong vessel.
expected_points: EDIT to change, DELETE to remove
answer: First, select 'Modify' or 'Delete' from the menu; Then, scroll through the list of entries; Next, confirm the modification or deletion. Do this correctly and the MMSI entry is successfully modified or deleted.

question: Demonstrate how to simulate a DSC test call and check that it is successful (simulator/training mode).
gold_answer: On the simulator or training mode, open DSC → TEST CALL, enter a coast station MMSI that supports automatic DSC test replies, and press SEND. Wait for the automated acknowledgement to appear in the log with the coast station's MMSI. Log the test date, time and result. In real operations, only send DSC test calls to stations that offer this service.
expected_points: target MMSI of coast station supporting test
log test date, time and result
answer: First, select the appropriate menu option for DSC self-test; Then, follow the on-screen instructions or procedure; Next, wait for the DSC to complete its self-test; After that, verify that the DSC indicates a successful self-test result. Do this correctly and the DSC confirms successful self-test completion. Just be careful: ensure the DSC is in the correct mode before initiating the self-test.

question: Show how to change the category of a DSC call (routine, safety, urgency) before sending.
gold_answer: During DSC call setup, before pressing SEND, use the up/down keys or a soft key to select the desired category — ROUTINE for normal traffic, SAFETY (SÉCURITÉ equivalent), URGENCY (PAN PAN equivalent) or DISTRESS for MAYDAY. The category determines the alarm behaviour on the receiving side and the channel priority. Verify the category on the display before SEND.
expected_points: change category during setup, before SEND
answer: First, select the appropriate category for the call; Then, send the DSC call. Do this correctly and the DSC call is sent with the correct category.

question: Demonstrate troubleshooting steps when DSC fails to send (e.g., no GPS, antenna/VSWR issues explained).
gold_answer: Check the display for error messages: NO GPS (enter manual position), NO MMSI (radio not configured), NO ACK (target station out of range or off), high VSWR / antenna warning (inspect antenna, coax, connectors). Verify supply voltage; low voltage may cause resets. Test on a working channel with a radio check. Log the fault and consult the manual or a marine electrician if unresolved.
expected_points: antenna/VSWR issues → inspect antenna and coax
low voltage → check battery and fuses
answer: DSC stands for Digital Selective Calling, and GPS integration is crucial for DSC functionality.

question: Show how to integrate DSC operation into a broader emergency drill involving EPIRB and AIS.
gold_answer: In the drill: (1) send a DSC distress alert on the simulator; (2) transmit voice MAYDAY on Ch 16; (3) simulate activating the EPIRB (using the built-in test only, never live); (4) confirm AIS-SART or AIS position transmission if fitted; (5) verify each system's watch and log entries. Debrief the crew on how the three systems complement each other: DSC alerts near vessels, EPIRB gives satellite backup, AIS-SART marks the raft.
answer: First, perform an emergency drill; Then, check the operational status of VHF/DSC equipment; Next, ensure EPIRB is properly stowed; After that, verify the AIS function. Do this correctly and all crew members are aware of their roles in an emergency situation. Just be careful: failure to follow these procedures may compromise safety during an emergency.

question: Demonstrate maintaining a DSC watch while simultaneously using voice channels.
gold_answer: The DSC watch on Ch 70 is automatic and independent of voice channel selection — the radio scans Ch 70 continuously. While transmitting or receiving voice on Ch 16 or any working channel, the DSC watch remains active in the background. Confirm the DSC watch indicator is displayed. Never disable the DSC watch except when the vessel is in port with the radio off.
expected_points: DSC watch on Ch 70 is automatic
runs in the background during voice traffic
confirm DSC watch indicator on display
never disable except when in port and radio off
answer: First, maintain a continuous watch on DSC Channel 70; Then, use Channel 16 for initial distress calls and nearby vessels; Next, use Channel 23 for distant vessels. Do this correctly and effective communication during emergencies while utilizing available resources efficiently. Just be careful: ensure to monitor the correct channels to avoid missing important communications.

question: Perform a brief explanation to the examiner of how DSC operations are tested in international SRC exams.
gold_answer: SRC exam DSC testing typically requires the candidate to demonstrate on a simulator: sending a DSC distress alert with correct nature and position, cancelling a false alert (DSC cancel + voice cancellation on Ch 16), initiating an INDIVIDUAL DSC routine call to a specified MMSI, interpreting a received DSC distress alert, and identifying the correct actions in Sea Area A1 (wait for coast station acknowledgement, log all details).
expected_points: send DSC distress with correct nature and position
INDIVIDUAL routine call to a specified MMSI
interpret a received DSC distress alert
answer: DSC stands for Digital Selective Calling, and MMSI is the Maritime Mobile Service Identity used for vessel identification.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate testing an EPIRB using the manufacturer's test function without triggering a real alert.
gold_answer: Locate the EPIRB's TEST button (often a separate small button or a press-and-hold sequence). Press as per manufacturer's instructions (typically 1-second press). Observe the test LED sequence and audible beep confirming battery, GPS lock (on GPS-equipped units) and self-test pass. Do NOT hold the button long enough to trigger a real 406 MHz transmission. Log the test date and result.
expected_points: observe test LED and audible sequence
do NOT trigger real 406 MHz transmission
answer: First, switch on the EPIRB; Then, check the battery status; Next, perform a self-test. Do this correctly and confirmation that the EPIRB is operational. Just be careful: ensure the antenna is clear of obstructions during testing.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to read and interpret the EPIRB label (MMSI/hex ID, expiry dates, registration info).
gold_answer: On the EPIRB label read: unique 15-character HEX ID (Cospas-Sarsat identity), MMSI (if configured), battery expiry date, hydrostatic release unit (HRU) expiry date, manufacturer, model, country code and registration reference. Verify the HEX ID matches your registration record. Expiry dates should be checked pre-departure and replaced when due — an out-of-date battery may fail during a real activation.
expected_points: match HEX ID to registration record
answer: First, read the EPIRB label; Then, note the MMSI/hex ID number; Next, check the expiry dates of the battery and antenna corrosion inhibitor; After that, update registration information if changed; Finally, ensure the EPIRB is properly stowed. Do this correctly and improved safety by ensuring the EPIRB is operational and registered. Just be careful: failure to maintain the EPIRB may compromise rescue efforts.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate checking the hydrostatic release unit (if fitted) for expiry date and condition.
gold_answer: Locate the HRU (hydrostatic release unit) attached to the EPIRB bracket. Read the expiry date stamped on the HRU housing — typically 2 years from manufacture. Inspect for corrosion, physical damage or salt build-up. If expiry is within 6 months or the HRU shows visible damage, replace it. Log the inspection and any replacement.
answer: First, check the hydrostatic release unit (HRU) for expiry date; Then, visually inspect the HRU for corrosion or expiry; Next, operate the HRU to ensure it functions correctly; After that, replace the HRU if expired or damaged. Do this correctly and the HRU is operational and ready for use in an emergency. Just be careful: failure of the HRU may result in loss of the liferaft.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to test a SART or AIS-SART in test mode according to instructions.
gold_answer: Remove the SART from its bracket. Follow the manufacturer's test procedure — typically press and hold the TEST button until the test LEDs sequence and an audible tone confirms success. For AIS-SART, some units display a TEST message. The test is normally brief (10–20 seconds) and does not transmit a real distress signal. Log the test date and result and return the unit to its bracket.
expected_points: test does not transmit real distress
log date and result, return to bracket
answer: First, turn the SART on; Then, wait two minutes; Next, check the display for a steady indication; After that, press and hold the TEST button for 5 seconds; Finally, observe the display during and after testing. Do this correctly and the SART will indicate a steady signal when turned on. Just be careful: ensure the SART is not in the water before turning it on.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to ensure NAVTEX or equivalent MSI receiver is set to relevant message categories and stations.
gold_answer: On the NAVTEX receiver open SETUP → STATIONS and select the stations that cover the intended sea area (identified by letter A–X). Then in CATEGORIES enable the relevant message categories — typically A (navigational warnings), B (meteorological), D (SAR), and disable those you don't need. Verify by observing incoming messages. Reconfigure when moving into a new sea area.
expected_points: CATEGORIES: enable A, B, D minimum
answer: First, ensure the NAVTEX or equivalent MSI receiver is set to the correct message category; Then, check that the receiver is tuned to the appropriate broadcast frequency. Do this correctly and the vessel receives timely and relevant navigational and meteorological information. Just be careful: ensure the receiver is properly configured to avoid missing important broadcasts.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to acknowledge a received NAVTEX safety message on the display and relate its contents.
gold_answer: NAVTEX messages appear on the display with station letter, category letter, message number and time. To "acknowledge", press READ or open the message; on many units this marks it as read and removes it from the unread queue. Read the content, note any effect on the passage plan, log a summary and (if useful) print the message. NAVTEX itself does not require you to transmit any acknowledgement.
expected_points: log summary and print if useful
answer: First, acknowledge receipt of the NAVTEX safety message; Then, read the message aloud including the issue time, position, and text. Do this correctly and mariners will be informed about safety messages affecting their area.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to check that GMDSS batteries are in good condition and properly charged (explanation and checks).
gold_answer: Check each battery-powered GMDSS item (portable VHF, EPIRB, PLB, SART, AIS-SART): battery expiry date on the label, no swelling or corrosion, terminal contacts clean. Where possible use the manufacturer's TEST function to confirm capacity. For rechargeable batteries verify a full charge and store on the charger. Log the check date. Replace any battery within 6 months of expiry.
expected_points: check expiry date on each battery
replace any battery within 6 months of expiry
answer: First, check the condition of GMDSS batteries; Then, ensure all batteries are fully charged; Next, replace any faulty or weak batteries; After that, check the watertightness of battery compartments; Finally, replace any corroded seals or gaskets; Then, check the operation of the battery cut-out relay; Then, check the operation of the under-voltage cut-out relay; Then, check the operation of the over-charge cut-out relay; Then, check the operation of the over-temperature cut-out relay; Then, check the operation of the over-current cut-out relay; Then, check the operation of the short-circuit protection device; Then, check the operation of the overload protection device; Then, check the operation of the fuses; Then, check the operation of the circuit breakers; Then, check the operation of the automatic voltage regulator; Then, check the operation of the manual voltage switch; Then, check the operation of the charger; Then, check the operation of the charger controller; Then, check the operation of the charger relay; Then, check the operation of the charger fuse; Then, check the operation of the charger circuit breaker; Then, check the operation of the charger output terminal; Then, check the operation of the charger input terminal; Then, check the operation of the charger control panel; Then, check the operation of the charger display; Then, check the operation of the charger alarm; Then, check the operation of the charger timer; Then, check the operation of the charger relay contact; Then, check the operation of the charger fuse holder; Then, check the operation of the charger circuit breaker holder; Then, check the operation of the charger output terminal holder; Then, check the operation of the charger input terminal holder; Then, check the operation of the charger control panel holder; Then, check the operation of the charger display holder; Then, check the operation of the charger alarm holder; Then, check the operation of the charger timer holder; Then, check the operation of the charger relay contact holder; Then, check the operation of the charger fuse holder holder; Then, check the operation of the charger circuit breaker holder holder; Then, check the operation of the charger output terminal holder holder; Then, check the operation of the charger input terminal holder holder; Then, check the operation of the charger control panel holder holder; Then, check the operation of the charger display holder holder; Then, check the operation of the charger alarm holder holder; Then, check the operation of the charger timer

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to store EPIRB and SART correctly for rapid deployment.
gold_answer: Stow the EPIRB in its dedicated bracket in an accessible location (usually near a companionway or on deck), with HRU armed. Stow SART/AIS-SART in bracket close to the liferaft or grab bag, quickly reachable. Both must be free of any covers that would prevent hydrostatic activation or manual removal. Include their location in the safety brief so any crew can retrieve them.
expected_points: EPIRB in dedicated bracket, HRU armed
SART near liferaft or grab bag
answer: First, stow the EPIRB in its dedicated bracket; Then, arm the hydrostatic release; Next, mount the SART at least 1 metre above the waterline; After that, keep the SART switched off until needed. Do this correctly and the EPIRB and SART are ready for immediate use in an emergency. Just be careful: ensure the SART is switched off until needed to prevent false alarms.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to launch a SART from its bracket in a simulated emergency.
gold_answer: Release the SART from its bracket (typically by rotating a lock or pressing a release). Extend the telescoping antenna to its full height. Activate per manufacturer's instructions (usually a switch or a press-and-hold). Hold as high as possible in the liferaft — a broomstick or paddle extension is recommended for maximum range. Once activated, do not switch off until rescue arrives or the battery expires.
expected_points: hold as high as possible in liferaft
do not switch off until rescue or battery expires
answer: First, pull the SART out of its bracket; Then, hold the SART vertically and activate it; Next, check that the SART is transmitting by looking for a steady light or by listening on channel 16. Do this correctly and the SART will transmit a signal to aid in search and rescue operations. Just be careful: ensure the SART is properly stowed before departure.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to integrate use of EPIRB and VHF DSC distress alert in an abandon-ship drill.
gold_answer: In the drill sequence: (1) send DSC distress alert with nature ABANDONING SHIP; (2) transmit voice MAYDAY on Ch 16 stating intention; (3) manually activate EPIRB (simulate; do NOT hold long enough for a real transmission); (4) take EPIRB, handheld VHF, SART and grab bag into the liferaft; (5) once in the raft, monitor Ch 16 on handheld and keep SART active. Debrief on sequence and roles.
expected_points: DSC distress with ABANDONING SHIP nature
take EPIRB, handheld VHF, SART, grab bag
monitor Ch 16 on handheld from raft
answer: First, sound the abandon-ship alarm; Then, inform the bridge / master; Next, operate the EPIRB / SART; After that, check the operation of VHF DSC. Do this correctly and all crew members are alerted to the emergency situation and can take appropriate action. Just be careful: ensure all crew members are accounted for during the abandon-ship process.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to interpret a NAVTEX message giving a navigational warning.
gold_answer: Read the header: station letter, category (A = navigational warning), message number and time. Read the body for area affected, position, description of the hazard, effect on shipping and any recommended action or route. Plot the hazard on the chart, note whether it affects the current or intended passage, and log a summary with actions taken (course change, extra watch).
expected_points: read header: station, category A, number, time
description of hazard and effect on shipping
log summary and any action taken
answer: First, read the message; Then, note the position and date of the navigational warning; Next, plot the area of the navigational warning on the chart; After that, join the ends of the arc or circle to form a closed shape; Finally, use a different colour pencil for the new information; Then, update the chart when the information is invalidated by a further broadcast. Do this correctly and improved situational awareness regarding navigational hazards. Just be careful: ensure to update charts promptly to avoid navigational risks.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to verify the correct registration of an EPIRB with national authorities (explained, with sample data).
gold_answer: Contact the national beacon registry (e.g. UK: The Beacon Registry, HM Coastguard; NL: Kustwacht Nederland) with the beacon's HEX ID. Verify that the registered owner, vessel details, 24/7 emergency contacts and beacon type match. Update any changes (ownership, contact numbers) immediately. Registration is normally free and can be checked online. An unregistered beacon delays SAR response significantly.
answer: First, register your 406 MHz EPIRB/PLB with HM Coastguard; Then, notify Ofcom of any changes regarding your EPIRB/PLB; Next, validate your registration every ten years; After that, check for free-of-charge upgrades to EPIRBs; Finally, ensure your EPIRB is properly registered and validated. Do this correctly and your EPIRB will be registered with HM Coastguard for search and rescue operations. Just be careful: failure to validate your registration may result in it being declared void.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to silence an accidentally activated EPIRB and report the false alert to authorities (simulated).
gold_answer: Turn the EPIRB switch back to OFF or return to its bracket according to model instructions. Immediately call the coastguard on Ch 16 or by phone: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), CANCEL FALSE EPIRB ALERT, HEX ID (…), TIME OF ACTIVATION (…), CAUSE (inadvertent), NO ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, OVER." Provide vessel details for cross-reference. Log the event. Confirm cancellation with the coastguard before ending contact.
expected_points: switch EPIRB off or return to bracket
call coastguard on Ch 16 or by phone
