state CANCEL FALSE EPIRB ALERT with HEX ID
give time and cause of activation
answer: First, silence the EPIRB; Then, report the false alert to the relevant Coastguard or Rescue Coordination Centre. Do this correctly and the incident is reported and resolved without causing unnecessary distress or resource allocation. Just be careful: accidental activation of an EPIRB can lead to unnecessary alerts and resource deployment.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to read off the battery expiry date on EPIRB and SART and record it in the log.
gold_answer: Locate the battery expiry label on the EPIRB (typically front or side panel) and on the SART (usually beside the manufacturer's label). Read the month and year (e.g. "BATTERY EXPIRES 08/2029"). Record both dates in the vessel's safety-equipment log, along with the inspection date. Set a calendar reminder for at least 6 months before each expiry so replacement can be arranged.
expected_points: locate expiry label on EPIRB and SART
set calendar reminder 6 months before expiry
answer: First, check the battery expiry date of the EPIRB; Then, note down the expiry date in the log; Next, replace the battery if it has expired. Do this correctly and the EPIRB remains operational until the next scheduled check. Just be careful: failure to replace the battery may result in non-operational equipment during an emergency.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to secure GMDSS equipment so that it remains usable after heavy weather.
gold_answer: Ensure EPIRB is firmly in its bracket with HRU armed but not obstructed. Store SART in a padded holder or bracket. Handheld VHF should be in a padded case, secured against sudden motion, in a location protected from spray. Grab bag containing spare batteries, PLBs and flares should be securely stowed near the companionway, waterproof and accessible with one hand. Do a pre-departure check on all fastenings.
expected_points: EPIRB firmly bracketed, HRU not obstructed
handheld VHF in padded case, protected from spray
answer: First, stow the VHF DSC equipment in its designated position; Then, secure the VHF DSC equipment with bungee cords or velcro; Next, stow the VHF equipment in its designated position; After that, secure the VHF equipment with bungee cords or velcro; Finally, stow the EPIRB and SART in their dedicated holders; Then, check the batteries of the EPIRB and SART for expiry dates. Do this correctly and all equipment is secured and ready for use during heavy weather. Just be careful: ensure all equipment is properly stowed and secured to prevent damage during heavy weather.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to incorporate GMDSS systems checks into a pre-voyage checklist.
gold_answer: Add to the pre-voyage checklist: (1) fixed VHF/DSC boot self-test, GPS position, correct MMSI; (2) handheld VHF battery and antenna; (3) EPIRB self-test and HRU condition; (4) SART self-test; (5) NAVTEX / MSI receiver on and receiving; (6) safety-equipment log up to date. Sign off each item before departure. This ensures that any pre-existing fault is caught in port, not at sea.
answer: First, perform regular systematic checks of GMDSS equipment; Then, include equipment checks in the muster list; Next, ensure the ship’s radio is always switched on and ready for use; After that, carry out systematic checks of the DSC and MF radio equipment; Finally, keep a log of all equipment checks. Do this correctly and improved safety through reliable communication capabilities. Just be careful: failure to maintain equipment can compromise safety during emergencies.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to retrieve and interpret AIS SAR target information relevant to a distress.
gold_answer: On the AIS display filter for SAR targets (typically shown as SAR aircraft symbol or SAR-SART marker). Select the target to view its MMSI, name, position, course, speed and CPA/TCPA. In a distress this shows where SAR units are and their ETA to the casualty. If the AIS is integrated with the VHF, an INDIVIDUAL DSC call can be initiated directly to the SAR unit's MMSI. Log the interaction.
expected_points: view MMSI, name, position, course, speed
integrated VHF can DSC-call the SAR unit
answer: First, select 'AIS' then 'SAR' from the menu; Then, read the information about the SAR target. Do this correctly and improved situational awareness regarding the location and status of the SAR target.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to combine voice, DSC, and GMDSS equipment in a coordinated SAR training scenario.
gold_answer: In the training scenario the on-scene actions run in parallel: DSC alert on the simulator, voice MAYDAY on Ch 16, EPIRB self-test, SART/AIS-SART in test mode, handheld VHF for the liferaft, and MRCC coordination on Ch 67 or working channel. One crew member is designated for each system so activities do not conflict. Debrief at the end to align system knowledge across the crew.
expected_points: DSC + voice MAYDAY + EPIRB + SART/AIS-SART + handheld
parallel actions with dedicated crew role each
MRCC coordination on a working channel
test modes only — no live transmissions
answer: First, transmit an urgency alert using DSC; Then, make a voice call to a coast station on channel 16; Next, transmit a safety message using voice on channel 70. Do this correctly and effective communication of urgent information and safety messages. Just be careful: ensure all equipment is properly configured and licensed for use.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate explaining to crew the basic functions of EPIRB and SART in a safety briefing.
gold_answer: Explain: "The EPIRB is our satellite-based distress beacon; when we activate it (or if it floats free with the HRU), it tells the Cospas-Sarsat satellites and MRCC where we are. The SART is a small radar responder we take into the liferaft; it makes us visible to any nearby SAR radar as a distinctive twelve-dot line. Location of each is here (show the bracket) and this is the manual activation button." Keep it under 3 minutes and end with a hands-on point-and-name test.
expected_points: EPIRB = satellite distress beacon via Cospas-Sarsat
answer: First, explain the function of the EPIRB; Then, demonstrate how to activate the SART; Next, discuss the importance of keeping the SART within reach during drills. Do this correctly and crew members will understand the functions of EPIRB and SART and know how to use them effectively. Just be careful: ensure the SART is turned off when not in use to conserve battery life.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to log all GMDSS system tests and maintenance actions in a structured way.
gold_answer: Maintain a GMDSS log with columns: date, system (VHF/DSC, EPIRB, SART, handheld, NAVTEX, AIS), test performed, result (pass/fail), any action taken, and signature of tester. Test intervals: weekly DSC check, monthly EPIRB and SART self-test, annual professional service. Keep the log with the ship station licence documents. This structured record supports insurance, coastguard audits and future incident reviews.
expected_points: date, system, test, result, action, signature
test intervals: weekly DSC, monthly EPIRB/SART
answer: First, log all system tests and maintenance actions; Then, note the result of each action; Next, indicate when the next test or check is due. Do this correctly and improved operational readiness and compliance with regulatory requirements. Just be careful: failure to log actions may lead to non-compliance.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Conduct a short radio conversation using correct "THIS IS", "OVER", and "OUT".
gold_answer: Example: "(Marina), (Marina), (Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), OVER." (Marina): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Marina), GO AHEAD, OVER." (Vessel): "(Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), REQUEST OVERNIGHT BERTH, ETA ONE SEVEN ZERO ZERO UTC, OVER." (Marina): "THIS IS (Marina), BERTH F THREE, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), BERTH F THREE, THANK YOU, OUT." Illustrates initial 3-3 identification, OVER between transmissions, THIS IS on continuations, and OUT to close.
expected_points: OUT to close with no reply expected
answer: First, initiate communication with 'MV Blue Horizon'; Then, request their current speed and destination; Next, acknowledge their response and state your own course and speed; After that, confirm you will maintain course and speed. Do this correctly and both vessels confirmed their intentions and agreed to maintain their respective courses and speeds.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate correcting a mistake mid-transmission using "CORRECTION".
gold_answer: Example: "THIS IS (Vessel), MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE WEST — CORRECTION, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE EAST, OVER." The pro-word CORRECTION explicitly voids the previous statement and signals the corrected version to follow.
expected_points: then the corrected word or phrase
answer: First, transmit 'CORRECTION'; Then, state the corrected part of the message; Next, continue with the rest of the message. Do this correctly and the recipient receives the corrected information.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to ask for repetition of a specific part of a message using "SAY AGAIN".
gold_answer: Options: "SAY AGAIN YOUR POSITION, OVER." "SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER 'PORT SIDE', OVER." "SAY AGAIN ALL BEFORE 'STARBOARD', OVER." "SAY AGAIN WORD BEFORE 'CHANNEL', OVER." Never use "repeat" — that is a military artillery pro-word. Structuring the request tells the other station exactly what to re-transmit and saves time.
answer: First, say 'SAY AGAIN' three times; Then, specify the part of the message to be repeated; Next, say 'REPEAT' followed by the part to be repeated. Do this correctly and the recipient repeats the specified part of the message clearly.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate placing another station on hold using "STANDBY" and then resuming communication.
gold_answer: Example: "(caller), THIS IS (own vessel), STANDBY, OVER." (Attend to the other task.) When ready to resume: "(caller), THIS IS (own vessel), OVER." (Caller): "(own vessel), THIS IS (caller), OVER." (Own vessel): "THIS IS (own vessel), CONTINUE WITH YOUR MESSAGE, OVER." STANDBY holds the channel; STANDBY OUT can be used to free the channel if the wait is longer.
expected_points: use STANDBY OUT if wait is longer
answer: First, place another station on hold; Then, resume communication when ready. Do this correctly and the communication is paused until the operator is ready to continue.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to acknowledge instructions clearly using "ROGER".
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Coastguard), REDUCE SPEED TO FIVE KNOTS, OVER." (Vessel): "(Coastguard), THIS IS (Vessel), ROGER, OVER." ROGER signals "received and understood" but implies no action commitment. If action is required and will be complied with, use WILCO instead. Do not combine as ROGER WILCO — it is redundant.
expected_points: does not imply action or agreement
answer: First, acknowledge the instruction; Then, repeat the instruction. Do this correctly and clear communication of the instruction.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate using "WILCO" correctly in response to an order.
gold_answer: Example: (Harbour Control): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Harbour), HOLD SOUTH OF NORTH ENTRANCE UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE, OVER." (Vessel): "(Harbour), THIS IS (Vessel), WILCO, OVER." WILCO ("WILL COMPLY") means received, understood and will carry out. Never combine with ROGER — WILCO already includes the meaning of ROGER.
expected_points: implies received, understood and will comply
use only when action will be taken
answer: The term 'WILCO' indicates a complete understanding of the order and confirmation to carry it out, and the response should include 'WILCO' followed by the repeated order.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to use "BREAK" to separate parts of a message during a longer transmission.
gold_answer: Example MAYDAY: "MAYDAY (vessel), POSITION FIVE ZERO ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE WEST, BREAK, NATURE OF DISTRESS FIRE ON BOARD, BREAK, POB FIVE, ONE INJURED, BREAK, ABANDONING TO LIFERAFT, OVER." BREAK marks logical separation between position, nature, POB and situation so the listener can copy each section.
expected_points: BREAK marks logical separation within one transmission
used inside MAYDAY between position, nature, POB, situation
answer: First, transmit 'BREAK'; Then, wait 15–20 seconds; Next, continue with the transmission after the break. Do this correctly and clear separation of different parts of the message.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate using "I SPELL" followed by phonetic spelling of a harbour name.
gold_answer: Example: "THIS IS (Vessel), DESTINATION SCHEVENINGEN, I SPELL SIERRA-CHARLIE-HOTEL-ECHO-VICTOR-ECHO-NOVEMBER-INDIA-NOVEMBER-GOLF-ECHO-NOVEMBER, SCHEVENINGEN, OVER." The plain word first tells the listener the pronunciation; I SPELL introduces the phonetic breakdown; the plain word after confirms the whole.
answer: First, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by the phonetic spelling of the word; Then, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by 'OVER'. Do this correctly and clear communication of the spelled word to the listening station.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to use "ALL STATIONS" at the start of a broadcast message.
gold_answer: Example SÉCURITÉ: "SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: (…), OUT." ALL STATIONS three times addresses every listener; it is used for MAYDAY, PAN PAN, SÉCURITÉ and general navigational broadcasts.
expected_points: used for MAYDAY, PAN PAN, SÉCURITÉ
followed by THIS IS + calling identity x3
answer: First, use 'ALL STATIONS' at the start of your broadcast; Then, say 'OUT' when finished with your message. Do this correctly and all stations within range will hear your message.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate ending a call correctly without saying "OVER AND OUT".
gold_answer: Correct endings: "THIS IS (Vessel), OUT." or "THIS IS (Vessel), STANDING BY ON CHANNEL ONE SIX, OUT." "OVER AND OUT" is a Hollywood invention combining two contradictory pro-words. OVER expects a reply; OUT ends the conversation. Choose one — usually OUT for the final transmission.
expected_points: end with OUT for final transmission
optionally state which channel you now monitor
answer: First, say 'OUT' to indicate the call is finished; Then, wait for the other station to respond before making another call. Do this correctly and the other station will understand that the conversation is complete and will not expect a response from you immediately.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to handle overlapping transmissions by using appropriate phrases to re-establish order.
gold_answer: If two stations transmit simultaneously and cannot be understood, the controlling station may say: "STATIONS CALLING (own vessel name), THIS IS (own vessel), CALL ONE AT A TIME, OVER." Each station then calls in turn. If two stations both realise they were transmitting, both should release PTT immediately, wait a couple of seconds, and let the called station identify who to call first.
expected_points: controlling station says STATIONS CALLING (name), CALL ONE AT A TIME
each station then calls in turn
short wait to reset the channel
answer: First, cease transmission; Then, wait one minute; Next, resume transmission. Do this correctly and communication is restored and all parties are informed of the need for clear communication.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate a short routine call including at least five correct pro-words.
gold_answer: Example: "(Marina), (Marina), (Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), OVER." (Marina): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Marina), GO AHEAD, OVER." (Vessel): "(Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), REQUEST BERTH FOR ONE NIGHT, ETA ONE SIX ZERO ZERO UTC, OVER." (Marina): "THIS IS (Marina), BERTH BAKER FIVE, I SPELL BRAVO ALFA KILO ECHO ROMEO, FIVE, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), ROGER, BERTH BAKER FIVE, THANK YOU, OUT." Uses: THIS IS, OVER, ROGER, I SPELL, OUT.
answer: First, transmit a short routine call; Then, wait for the other station to respond; Next, transmit a question on the same channel; After that, listen for a reply. Do this correctly and the other station responds to the call.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to politely decline a request using clear, standard phraseology.
gold_answer: Example: "(other vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), NEGATIVE, UNABLE TO PROVIDE TOW DUE TO ADVERSE SEA STATE AND OWN VESSEL SAFETY, RECOMMEND YOU CONTACT COASTGUARD ON CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER." NEGATIVE is the standard refusal; providing a specific reason and a suggested alternative keeps the exchange helpful and factual.
expected_points: suggest an alternative (e.g. coastguard, other vessel)
answer: First, respond with 'I will not do that'; Then, say 'No, I cannot ...'; Next, state 'That is not possible'. Do this correctly and the other party understands your limitations clearly. Just be careful: ensure clarity in communication to avoid misunderstandings.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate hearing a poorly transmitted message and requesting a repeat using standard words.
gold_answer: Example: "(other station), THIS IS (own vessel), YOUR SIGNAL IS UNREADABLE, SAY AGAIN YOUR ENTIRE MESSAGE, OVER." Or more specific: "YOUR SIGNAL IS BROKEN, SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER 'POSITION', OVER." Standard phraseology (SAY AGAIN, SIGNAL UNREADABLE / BROKEN) tells the other station exactly what is needed.
answer: First, say 'Repeat ...'; Then, say 'Say again (please)'. Do this correctly and the listener can obtain clarification of the poorly transmitted message.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to confirm understanding of a complex instruction by repeating it back ("readback").
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Coastguard), PROCEED TO POSITION FIVE ZERO ONE TWO NORTH ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE WEST, HOLD AT REDUCED SPEED, MONITOR CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER." (Vessel): "(Coastguard), THIS IS (Vessel), READBACK: PROCEED TO POSITION FIVE ZERO ONE TWO NORTH ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE WEST, HOLD AT REDUCED SPEED, MONITOR CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER." Coastguard confirms with ROGER.
expected_points: allows the sender to confirm accuracy
standard SMCP practice for complex instructions
answer: First, repeat the instruction; Then, say 'I understand'; Next, say 'Out'. Do this correctly and confirmation of understanding without ambiguity.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate using "AFFIRMATIVE" and "NEGATIVE" clearly instead of "YES" or "NO".
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Coastguard), CONFIRM YOU HAVE FIVE PERSONS ON BOARD, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), AFFIRMATIVE, POB FIVE, OVER." And: "(Vessel), CONFIRM YOU HAVE MEDICAL EMERGENCY, OVER." (Vessel): "NEGATIVE, NO MEDICAL EMERGENCY, OVER." These words are noise-resistant and unambiguous.
expected_points: preferred over YES / NO on radio
answer: First, respond with 'AFFIRMATIVE' for yes; Then, respond with 'NEGATIVE' for no; Next, use 'WILCO' when acknowledging clear understanding; After that, use 'I SPELL' before spelling out words. Do this correctly and improved clarity in communication.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to manage a handover of communication from one officer to another over the radio.
gold_answer: Example: "(Coastguard), THIS IS (Vessel), COMMUNICATIONS OFFICER HANDING OVER TO SKIPPER, STAND BY, OVER." On resumption: "(Coastguard), THIS IS (Vessel), SKIPPER NOW ON THE RADIO, OVER." Log the handover time and the identity of the new operator. Notify any coordinating station so they know who they are talking to. On short exchanges the same operator normally stays on the radio.
expected_points: identify the new operator on resumption
answer: First, confirm the handover with the relieving officer; Then, read out the watch face and time; Next, state the last position and course; After that, report the next position and course; Finally, state the ETA at the next waypoint or at the pilot station; Then, state the ETA at the anchorage or berth; Then, state the strength of the current; Then, state the wind direction and force; Then, state the sea conditions; Then, state the visibility; Then, state the traffic situation; Then, state the weather forecast; Then, state the navigational warnings. Do this correctly and both officers are informed about the current status of the vessel and can effectively communicate with each other.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate how to indicate the end of a broadcast message where no reply is expected.
gold_answer: For broadcasts (SÉCURITÉ, MAYDAY RELAY, MSI), end with OUT rather than OVER, since no direct reply from a specific station is expected. Example: "...VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, THIS IS (Vessel), OUT." This tells all listeners the transmission is complete. If clarifications are invited on a working channel, mention it: "...CLARIFICATIONS ON CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OUT."
expected_points: no reply from specific station expected
optionally invite clarifications on working channel
OVER would incorrectly imply awaited reply
answer: First, use 'OUT' to indicate the end of a broadcast message; Then, say 'OVER' and wait for a reply. Do this correctly and clear communication of message boundaries.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to phrase a message so that the "who, where, what" structure is clear and concise.
gold_answer: Example: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel) [WHO], APPROACHING FROM SOUTH ENTRANCE [WHERE], REQUEST PERMISSION TO ENTER AND BERTH IN VISITOR AREA [WHAT], ETA ONE SIX ZERO ZERO UTC [WHEN], OVER." Each element is short and complete. This structure lets the harbour master respond in a single transmission with clearance and berth assignment.
expected_points: WHO – both station names and vessel identity
short and complete for a single-response reply
answer: First, state the name of your vessel; Then, state the name of their vessel; Next, state the position of your vessel; After that, state the position of their vessel; Finally, state the action you will take; Then, state the time when you will pass. Do this correctly and both vessels have a clear understanding of each other's positions and intentions.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Conduct a short multi-step scenario where proper use of procedure words prevents misunderstanding.
gold_answer: Scenario: berthing exchange in poor visibility. (Vessel): "(Harbour), (Harbour), (Harbour), THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), OVER." (Harbour): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Harbour), GO AHEAD, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), TWELVE METRES LOA, VISIBILITY ONE HUNDRED METRES, REQUEST GUIDANCE FOR BERTHING, OVER." (Harbour): "THIS IS (Harbour), PROCEED TO WAITING PONTOON, TURN STARBOARD AT NORTH CARDINAL, I SPELL WHISKEY PAPA, OVER." (Vessel): "READBACK: WAITING PONTOON, TURN STARBOARD AT NORTH CARDINAL WHISKEY PAPA, OVER." (Harbour): "ROGER, OUT." Use of THIS IS, OVER, I SPELL, READBACK, ROGER and OUT keeps this potentially hazardous exchange unambiguous.
answer: First, request confirmation of message read; Then, state 'I confirm' followed by the confirmed part of the message; Next, state 'I do not confirm' followed by the unconfirmed part of the message. Do this correctly and both parties have a clear understanding of the communicated information.

question: Spell the vessel's name on request using the phonetic alphabet.
gold_answer: Example for vessel PEGASUS: "THIS IS SAILING VESSEL PEGASUS, I SPELL PAPA-ECHO-GOLF-ALFA-SIERRA-UNIFORM-SIERRA, PEGASUS, OVER." The plain word first indicates pronunciation; I SPELL introduces the phonetic breakdown; the plain word after confirms the whole.
expected_points: include OVER or full station identification
answer: The vessel's name must be spelled using the phonetic alphabet, and the phonetic alphabet includes words like Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, etc.

question: Spell your own surname and first name using the phonetic alphabet.
gold_answer: Example surname SMITH, first name JOHN: "SURNAME SMITH, I SPELL SIERRA-MIKE-INDIA-TANGO-HOTEL, SMITH. FIRST NAME JOHN, I SPELL JULIETT-OSCAR-HOTEL-NOVEMBER, JOHN. OVER." Spelling both is essential in SAR to ensure hospitals, embassies and next-of-kin records are accurate.
expected_points: state plain surname and first name
answer: The phonetic alphabet is used to spell letters clearly over the radio, and each letter has a specific code word to avoid confusion.

question: Spell the port of destination using phonetic letters.
gold_answer: Example destination BREST: "THIS IS (Vessel), DESTINATION BREST, I SPELL BRAVO-ROMEO-ECHO-SIERRA-TANGO, BREST, OVER." Especially important for ports whose names are not English (Brest, Calais, IJmuiden, Vigo) where non-native listeners could easily misread them.
expected_points: essential for foreign or non-English port names
answer: First, spell the name using phonetic alphabet; Then, read back the spelled name for confirmation. Do this correctly and clear communication of the vessel's name.

question: Spell the MMSI "211450001" digit by digit using correct number pronunciation.
gold_answer: "MMSI TWO-ONE-ONE-FOWER-FIFE-ZERO-ZERO-ZERO-ONE." Digit by digit, with FOWER for 4, FIFE for 5, ZERO for 0. Speak clearly with a short pause between groups (e.g. after the first three MID digits). Do not read "211" as "two hundred and eleven" — digit-by-digit prevents confusion.
answer: First, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by the phonetic spelling of each digit; Then, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by 'I SAY'. Do this correctly and clear communication of the MMSI number.

question: Spell a waypoint name (given by examiner) that is difficult to understand over radio.
gold_answer: Example waypoint TX3 (given by examiner): "WAYPOINT TX3, I SPELL TANGO-XRAY, THREE, TX3, OVER." For a longer name like GRAVELINES: "GRAVELINES, I SPELL GOLF-ROMEO-ALFA-VICTOR-ECHO-LIMA-INDIA-NOVEMBER-ECHO-SIERRA, GRAVELINES, OVER." Combine plain name, I SPELL, phonetic and readback for any name likely to be misheard.
answer: First, spell the waypoint name using phonetic alphabet; Then, read back the spelled name for confirmation. Do this correctly and clear communication of the waypoint name.

question: Demonstrate reading back a spelled-out word from another station to confirm accurate reception.
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "MEDICAL CONDITION IS ANGINA, I SPELL ALFA-NOVEMBER-GOLF-INDIA-NOVEMBER-ALFA, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), READBACK ANGINA, I SPELL ALFA-NOVEMBER-GOLF-INDIA-NOVEMBER-ALFA, ANGINA, OVER." The coastguard then confirms with ROGER. Readback ensures both stations have identical wording of a critical term.
expected_points: I SPELL with same phonetic letters
await confirmation from the other station
answer: First, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by the phonetic spelling of the word; Then, transmit 'I SPELL' again followed by 'OVER'. Do this correctly and the other station confirms receipt of the spelled-out word.

question: Spell the vessel's call sign combining letters and numbers.
gold_answer: Example call sign 2ABC5: "CALL SIGN TWO-ALFA-BRAVO-CHARLIE-FIVE" or fully phrased: "THIS IS (Vessel), CALL SIGN TWO, I SPELL ALFA-BRAVO-CHARLIE, FIVE, OVER." Each character is spoken separately, letters with phonetic words and digits with radiotelephony pronunciation. Do not try to read the call sign as a word.
expected_points: brief pause between groups if helpful
answer: First, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by 'PAN-PAN'; Then, spell the vessel's name using phonetic alphabet; Next, say 'I SPELL' again followed by 'OUT'. Do this correctly and other vessels will understand the spelling of the vessel's name.

question: Spell "MAYDAY" and "PAN PAN" when requested.
gold_answer: MAYDAY: MIKE-ALFA-YANKEE-DELTA-ALFA-YANKEE. PAN PAN: PAPA-ALFA-NOVEMBER, PAPA-ALFA-NOVEMBER. Note that in practice these prefixes are transmitted as words (MAYDAY x3, PAN PAN x3) not letter by letter. Being able to spell them accurately confirms familiarity with the phonetic alphabet.
expected_points: MAYDAY = MIKE ALFA YANKEE DELTA ALFA YANKEE
words are the prefixes themselves in practice
answer: The word 'Mayday' comes from the French word 'm'aidez' meaning 'help me', and a 'Securité' call is used to alert other vessels of navigational hazards or important safety information.

question: Demonstrate giving a latitude and longitude including degrees and minutes using words and numbers.
gold_answer: Example: "LATITUDE FIVE ZERO DEGREES ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE MINUTES NORTH, LONGITUDE ZERO ZERO ONE DEGREES FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE MINUTES WEST, OVER." Digit by digit; use DECIMAL not POINT; state DEGREES, MINUTES and hemisphere (NORTH/SOUTH, EAST/WEST) in plain language.
expected_points: DEGREES and MINUTES stated in plain language
answer: First, give latitude and longitude; Then, state the bearing and distance of the nearest land or navigation mark; Next, provide UTC time and tidal predictions; After that, report wind direction and force; Finally, indicate sea conditions; Then, state visibility and cloud cover; Then, mention any other relevant information. Do this correctly and improved situational awareness for all onboard.

question: Spell the name of a local hazard (e.g., "ROCKY SHOAL") so another vessel can note it correctly.
gold_answer: Example: "HAZARD NAME ROCKY SHOAL, I SPELL ROMEO-OSCAR-CHARLIE-KILO-YANKEE, ROCKY, SIERRA-HOTEL-OSCAR-ALFA-LIMA, SHOAL, OVER." Two-word hazard names are spelled as two separate I SPELL sequences with a brief pause between. This lets the receiving station write each word correctly.
expected_points: clear pronunciation of the whole name
answer: The name of the hazard is read out letter by letter, and using 'I SPELL' indicates the beginning and end of the spelling.

question: Practice changing from normal speech to phonetic spelling and back smoothly in one transmission.
gold_answer: Example: "THIS IS (Vessel), WE ARE HEADING FOR CALSHOT, I SPELL CHARLIE-ALFA-LIMA-SIERRA-HOTEL-OSCAR-TANGO, CALSHOT, ETA ONE FIVE THREE ZERO UTC, OVER." The transition is signalled by the plain word first, I SPELL, then phonetic, then plain word again — after which normal speech continues seamlessly.
answer: First, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by the phonetic spelling of the word; Then, transmit 'I SPELL' again followed by 'OVER'. Do this correctly and the recipient can accurately spell out the word without confusion.

question: Spell the name of a crew member to be evacuated to ensure hospital receives the correct details.
gold_answer: Example crew member ANDERSON, first name PAUL: "CASUALTY SURNAME ANDERSON, I SPELL ALFA-NOVEMBER-DELTA-ECHO-ROMEO-SIERRA-OSCAR-NOVEMBER, ANDERSON. FIRST NAME PAUL, I SPELL PAPA-ALFA-UNIFORM-LIMA, PAUL. AGE FIVE FOUR YEARS, MALE, OVER." Spelling both names is essential in SAR / MEDEVAC so hospital and family records are correct.
expected_points: critical for hospital and family records
answer: First, spell the name; Then, read back the spelled name. Do this correctly and the hospital receives the correct spelling of the crew member's name.

question: Spell a medical condition name provided by the examiner for a MEDICO scenario.
gold_answer: Example condition APPENDICITIS: "SUSPECTED CONDITION APPENDICITIS, I SPELL ALFA-PAPA-PAPA-ECHO-NOVEMBER-DELTA-INDIA-CHARLIE-INDIA-TANGO-INDIA-SIERRA, APPENDICITIS, OVER." Medical condition names are often unfamiliar to non-native speakers; spelling ensures a correct link to the duty doctor's diagnosis and advice.
answer: The examiner provides a condition name, and the operator must spell the condition using phonetic alphabet.

question: Spell the name of your marina or yacht club clearly for a radio log or report.
gold_answer: Example: "MARINA CROUCH HARBOUR, I SPELL CHARLIE-ROMEO-OSCAR-UNIFORM-CHARLIE-HOTEL, CROUCH, HOTEL-ALFA-ROMEO-BRAVO-OSCAR-UNIFORM-ROMEO, HARBOUR, OVER." Two-word names get two separate I SPELL sequences. This makes the log entry unambiguous.
answer: The name should be spelled out clearly using phonetic alphabet, and the number should be read digit by digit.

question: Spell a buoy identification code (e.g., "BF3") using phonetic and number words.
gold_answer: Example: "BUOY BF3, I SPELL BRAVO-FOXTROT, THREE, BF3, OVER." Letters spelled phonetically, digits with radiotelephony pronunciation. The plain code before and after the spelling confirms the whole.
answer: First, spell the identification code; Then, read back the spelled code. Do this correctly and the communication is clear regarding the buoy's identity.

question: Demonstrate confirming a spelled-out course (e.g., "course 2 - 7 - 0") with readback.
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Coastguard), STEER COURSE TWO-SEVEN-ZERO, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), READBACK: STEER COURSE TWO-SEVEN-ZERO, OVER." (Coastguard): "ROGER, OUT." Each digit spoken separately; readback confirms accurate reception of a course that could otherwise be misheard as 220, 250 or 290.
expected_points: digit by digit for the course
answer: First, transmit 'I SPELL'; Then, spell the word phonetically; Next, transmit 'I SPELL' again followed by 'OVER'. Do this correctly and clear communication of the spelled-out word.

question: Spell the word "ANCHORAGE" on request.
gold_answer: "ANCHORAGE, I SPELL ALFA-NOVEMBER-CHARLIE-HOTEL-OSCAR-ROMEO-ALFA-GOLF-ECHO, ANCHORAGE, OVER." Plain word first, I SPELL, phonetic letters, plain word again. Standard technique for any unfamiliar or long English word.
expected_points: ALFA NOVEMBER CHARLIE HOTEL OSCAR ROMEO ALFA GOLF ECHO
answer: The word 'ANCHORAGE' is spelled out letter by letter, and the phonetic alphabet is used to spell each letter clearly.

question: Spell the name of a nearby vessel with a similar-sounding name to your own.
gold_answer: Example own vessel SEAWIND, nearby vessel SEAWEED: "NEARBY VESSEL SEAWEED, I SPELL SIERRA-ECHO-ALFA-WHISKEY-ECHO-ECHO-DELTA, SEAWEED, OVER." The phonetic spelling makes the distinction between similar-sounding names explicit so MRCC or the coastguard cannot confuse the two.
expected_points: essential when own and other vessel names are similar
answer: First, spell the name using phonetic alphabet; Then, read back the spelled name for confirmation. Do this correctly and both vessels confirm the correct name was communicated.

question: Demonstrate teaching another crew member the phonetic alphabet in a short coaching scenario.
gold_answer: Sit at the radio and hand the crew member the laminated phonetic-alphabet card. Ask them to spell three easy items (the vessel's name, the port of destination, their own surname) and give positive feedback. Then run a mock exchange where you request a spelled position: "SAY AGAIN AND SPELL YOUR POSITION." Keep the coaching under 10 minutes and end with a hands-on drill.
expected_points: practise on vessel name, destination and own surname
mock exchange with SAY AGAIN AND SPELL
answer: First, write down the phonetic alphabet; Then, practice spelling using the phonetic alphabet; Next, teach a crew member how to spell using the phonetic alphabet. Do this correctly and improved communication skills through effective spelling.

question: Perform a short simulated exchange where correct phonetic spelling prevents a navigational error.
gold_answer: Scenario: pilotage instruction from harbour to a small vessel. (Harbour): "(Vessel), STEER FOR NORTH CARDINAL WHISKEY PAPA, I SPELL WHISKEY-PAPA, THEN TURN STARBOARD INTO WEST HARBOUR, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), READBACK: STEER FOR NORTH CARDINAL WHISKEY PAPA, THEN TURN STARBOARD INTO WEST HARBOUR, OVER." (Harbour): "ROGER, OUT." Without the phonetic spelling of WP, the vessel could confuse it with WB, WD or KP and steer for a wrong buoy — potentially into shoal water.
expected_points: harbour uses I SPELL for buoy label
phonetic prevents confusion of similar letters
prevents grounding on wrong-buoy navigation error
answer: First, transmit 'I SPELL' followed by the phonetic spelling of the word; Then, transmit 'I SPELL' again followed by the phonetic spelling of the number. Do this correctly and clear communication of the spelled word or number to avoid navigational errors.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Conduct a complete simulated MAYDAY exchange with MRCC from initial alert to coordination of assistance.
gold_answer: Sequence: (1) DSC distress alert on Ch 70 with nature and position; (2) voice MAYDAY on Ch 16 with full standard message (identity, position, nature, assistance, POB, OVER); (3) MRCC acknowledges and asks for follow-up detail (POB, injuries, safety equipment); (4) MRCC tasks assisting vessels and/or SAR units; (5) periodic updates on situation; (6) shift to working channel if MRCC directs; (7) situation resolved and MRCC terminates with SEELONCE FEENEE. All exchanges logged with UTC time.
expected_points: tasks assisting vessels and SAR units
periodic updates and shift to working channel
answer: First, transmit a DSC distress alert; Then, watch the radar and report; Next, stand by navigation equipment; After that, stand by engine room; Finally, request assistance; Then, report ETA at distress position; Then, report position of vessel(s) in vicinity; Then, report condition of persons on board. Do this correctly and MRCC acknowledges the distress alert and coordinates search and rescue efforts. Just be careful: ensure all safety equipment is operational.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Perform a PAN PAN call regarding a crew member with a suspected broken arm, then coordinate medical advice.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "PAN PAN MEDICO x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), MEDICAL: MALE CREW MEMBER AGED THREE FIVE, FELL FROM STEP, SUSPECTED FRACTURE RIGHT FOREARM, CONSCIOUS, STABLE, WEARING LIFE JACKET, REQUEST MEDICAL ADVICE, POB FOUR, OVER." MRCC responds, may link to duty doctor who will give first-aid and evacuation advice. Follow instructions and log everything.
expected_points: PAN PAN MEDICO x3, ALL STATIONS x3
request medical advice; MRCC connects duty doctor
answer: First, perform a PAN PAN call; Then, broadcast 'Mayday, Mayday, Mayday'; Next, provide your position, the nature of your urgent problem, and what assistance you need. Do this correctly and the Coast Guard will respond to the distress call and provide necessary assistance. Just be careful: do not use 'Mayday' unless there is immediate danger to life.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Demonstrate using VHF to coordinate with a nearby vessel assisting you in a man-overboard recovery.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 (or an assigned working channel): "(other vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), MAN OVERBOARD AT POSITION (…), TIME OF FALL (…), OUR ETA TO POSITION (…), REQUEST YOU JOIN SEARCH FROM (direction), USE PARALLEL TRACKS AT (spacing), OVER." Update every couple of minutes. If you have not already, send DSC distress with appropriate nature and voice MAYDAY to alert MRCC.
answer: First, acknowledge the incoming call and confirm the ability to assist; Then, request the other vessel to maintain course and speed while you maneuver; Next, inform the other vessel of your intention to alter course and speed; After that, thank the other vessel for their assistance and confirm your course alteration. Do this correctly and both vessels agreed on the course of action for the man-overboard recovery. Just be careful: ensure safe distance and communication to avoid collision.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Show how to request immediate towing assistance while clearly stating the risks if not assisted.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "PAN PAN x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), URGENCY: TOTAL ENGINE FAILURE, DRIFTING AT ONE POINT FIVE KNOTS TOWARDS LEE SHORE THREE MILES DISTANT, ESTIMATED GROUNDING IN NINETY MINUTES IF NO ASSISTANCE, REQUEST TOW, POB FOUR, OVER." Provide clear time-to-hazard so MRCC can prioritise appropriately.
expected_points: PAN PAN x3, ALL STATIONS x3
answer: First, request immediate towing assistance; Then, state the number of crew members on board; Next, specify the type of assistance required; After that, indicate the risk of pollution; Finally, provide the ETA of the tug. Do this correctly and the vessel receives timely assistance, potentially averting a pollution incident. Just be careful: failure to act may result in environmental pollution.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Perform a SECURITÉ warning about a dangerous object adrift on your planned route.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: LARGE STEEL DRUM SIGHTED IN POSITION (lat/long), APPROXIMATELY TWO METRES DIAMETER, PARTIALLY SUBMERGED, DRIFTING NORTH-EAST, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, OUT." Follow up with coastguard on their working channel for rebroadcast.
expected_points: give hazard position and observation time
advise vessels to keep clear; follow up with coastguard
answer: First, perform a SECURITÉ warning; Then, broadcast the position and details of the dangerous object; Next, state the intention to keep clear. Do this correctly and other vessels are informed of the danger and can take appropriate action to avoid collision. Just be careful: keep clear of the dangerous object.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Demonstrate updating the coastguard about worsening weather conditions experienced on scene.
gold_answer: On the coastguard working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), UPDATE ON WEATHER — WIND NOW WEST-SOUTH-WEST FIVE ZERO KNOTS GUSTING SIX ZERO, SEA STATE ROUGH, VISIBILITY LESS THAN ONE MILE IN HEAVY RAIN, CONDITIONS EXCEED FORECAST FOR THIS AREA, OVER." Coastguard may include this in the next SÉCURITÉ broadcast and adjust SAR asset tasking. Log the exchange.
expected_points: state wind, sea, visibility, deviations from forecast
answer: First, update coastguard with current position; Then, advise coastguard if unable to proceed; Next, inform coastguard of ETA at next waypoint; After that, report if weather worsens; Finally, state if unable to maintain course or speed; Then, advise if unable to take further instructions. Do this correctly and the coastguard is informed of the vessel's status and can provide appropriate assistance. Just be careful: unable to maintain course or speed may indicate a need for immediate assistance.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Show how to use VHF to coordinate with harbour control to give priority for an emergency entry.
gold_answer: On port control channel: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (vessel), PAN PAN — REQUEST PRIORITY ENTRY, MEDICAL EMERGENCY ON BOARD, PATIENT (age, sex, condition), POB (…), POSITION (…), ETA HARBOUR ENTRANCE ONE FIVE MINUTES, OVER." Harbour control may hold other traffic, direct straight to the emergency berth or ambulance pontoon, and coordinate with ambulance services on shore. Log all instructions.
expected_points: harbour control coordinates berth and ambulance
answer: First, contact harbour control; Then, request to put you through to the coastguard; Next, state your position and emergency nature; After that, ask if they can put you through to the coastguard; Finally, confirm with the coastguard that they will call you back. Do this correctly and the coastguard is informed of the emergency and will call back when they can. Just be careful: ensure to communicate clearly and promptly to avoid delays in receiving assistance.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Perform a short exchange reporting smoke observed from another vessel and your intention to investigate.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REPORTING SMOKE FROM VESSEL IN POSITION (…), BEARING (…) FROM MY POSITION, DISTANCE (…), I INTEND TO CLOSE AND INVESTIGATE, WILL UPDATE IN FIVE MINUTES, OVER." Coastguard acknowledges. Approach with caution, keep listening watch on Ch 16, and report findings promptly. If it is a fire, be prepared to escalate to MAYDAY RELAY on their behalf.
expected_points: escalate to MAYDAY RELAY if needed
answer: First, report smoke observed from MV Ocean Breeze; Then, acknowledge MV Ocean Breeze's response and state intention to investigate further. Do this correctly and both vessels confirmed the situation and agreed on the course of action. Just be careful: ensure safety while investigating potential hazards.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Demonstrate giving a clear and concise position using both GPS format and visual references.
gold_answer: Example: "POSITION FIVE ZERO ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE MINUTES NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE MINUTES WEST, TWO POINT FIVE MILES SOUTH OF ANVIL POINT LIGHT, BEARING ZERO ONE ZERO DEGREES FROM THE LIGHT." Two independent forms — GPS and visual bearing/distance from a chart feature — protect against a single-source error.
expected_points: visual bearing and distance from a fixed feature
answer: First, provide latitude and longitude in degree-minute-second format; Then, state the reference datum for latitude and longitude; Next, give the distance and bearing to a landmark or waypoint. Do this correctly and the listener can accurately determine the vessel's position. Just be careful: ensure the position is given relative to a known reference point.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Show how to report a near-miss collision incident in a factual way over VHF.
gold_answer: On the coastguard working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REPORTING NEAR-MISS COLLISION AT (position), TIME (UTC), WITH VESSEL (name / callsign / MMSI if known), OUR COURSE (…) SPEED (…), OTHER VESSEL'S APPARENT COURSE (…) SPEED (…), CLOSEST APPROACH APPROXIMATELY (distance), NO DAMAGE, WISH TO REPORT FOR THE RECORD, OVER." Coastguard logs the report; may follow up formally.
answer: First, report the near-miss collision; Then, provide your position and course; Next, acknowledge their position and course. Do this correctly and both vessels are informed of the near-miss situation and can take appropriate actions. Just be careful: maintain safe navigation to avoid further incidents.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Perform a conversation where you must advise another small vessel to alter course for safety.
gold_answer: On Ch 13 (bridge-to-bridge) or Ch 16: "(other vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), ADVICE: I RECOMMEND YOU ALTER COURSE TO STARBOARD, SEA ROOM AHEAD LIMITED BY OFF-LYING ROCKS, ALTERNATIVE TRACK AVAILABLE VIA (…), OVER." Uses SMCP message marker ADVICE. Be clear you are advising, not instructing (unless you are the controlling station); accept their decision.
expected_points: offer alternative track and accept their decision
answer: First, hailed MV Sea Explorer to confirm awareness of their position; Then, acknowledged MV Sea Explorer's response and stated intention to maintain course and speed; Next, informed MV Sea Explorer that their position is unsafe and requested immediate action. Do this correctly and both vessels acknowledged the situation, with MV Sea Explorer being advised to take immediate action to avoid collision. Just be careful: the position of MV Sea Explorer is unsafe and may lead to a collision if no action is taken.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Demonstrate how to respond to a safety broadcast altering the recommended route into a harbour.
gold_answer: On receipt of the SÉCURITÉ broadcast, log the changed route, plot the new track on the chart, brief the crew and call harbour control on the port channel: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (vessel), UNDERSTAND ROUTE ALTERED VIA (new route), REQUEST CONFIRMATION AND ANY ADDITIONAL INSTRUCTIONS, OVER." Harbour control confirms, adds any specific holding points or speed restrictions. Log the exchange.
expected_points: call harbour control to confirm new route
note additional holding or speed instructions
answer: First, acknowledge the safety broadcast; Then, plot the new route on the chart; Next, adjust the planned voyage to avoid the reported area; After that, inform the master or skipper about the situation; Finally, stand by for further instructions. Do this correctly and the vessel will be aware of the navigational hazards and will take appropriate measures to ensure safety. Just be careful: do not navigate in the reported area until further notice.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Show how to coordinate with SAR units approaching from different directions.
gold_answer: On the SAR working channel (or Ch 16 if not assigned): "(SAR UNIT), THIS IS (vessel), MY POSITION (…), COURSE (…), SPEED (…), VISUAL CONTACT WITH LIFEBOAT (name) BEARING ZERO ONE ZERO, DISTANCE ONE MILE, AND HELICOPTER (name) TO THE NORTH-WEST, I WILL MAINTAIN CURRENT COURSE, OVER." This picture-building lets the SAR units and MRCC deconflict approaches, avoid collision and coordinate on-scene actions.
expected_points: identify visible SAR units and bearings
answer: First, report your position; Then, report your present course and speed; Next, report your ETA at the meeting point; After that, acknowledge their ETA and state your intention to wait; Finally, confirm you will keep clear until they are alongside. Do this correctly and both vessels will coordinate their actions for safe navigation. Just be careful: ensure to keep clear of the other vessel until it is alongside.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Perform an exchange where you explain to MRCC why you are unable to assist another vessel due to your own safety limitations.
gold_answer: On the coastguard channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REGARDING MAYDAY OF (time) FROM (vessel name), UNABLE TO PROCEED TO ASSIST — MY OWN VESSEL IS SEVERELY REEFED IN GALE FORCE 8, LEE SHORE THREE MILES DOWNWIND, OWN CREW EXHAUSTED, RISK TO OWN VESSEL, REQUESTING RELEASE FROM DUTY, OVER." Coastguard formally releases you from the duty. Log the reason clearly for the record.
expected_points: identify the distress you are referring to
answer: First, acknowledge MRCC's call and state inability to assist; Then, inform MRCC of the other vessel's condition and request for assistance; Next, confirm awareness of the situation and state inability to assist further. Do this correctly and MRCC is informed of the situation and the vessel's inability to assist. Just be careful: do not attempt to assist another vessel if it poses a danger to your own safety.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Demonstrate using radio to organise evacuation of a sick crew member to a rescue boat.
gold_answer: On coordinated channel with SAR: "(RESCUE BOAT), THIS IS (vessel), CASUALTY READY FOR TRANSFER, WE WILL COME ONTO PORT TACK AT REDUCED SPEED FOR TRANSFER, CASUALTY IN LIFE JACKET AND SLING, TWO CREW HELPING, YOU COME ALONGSIDE PORT SIDE MIDSHIPS, OVER." Coordinate speed, side, personnel and equipment before the transfer starts. Keep radio contact continuous during the handover.
answer: First, call the coastguard on VHF Channel 16; Then, inform the master or chief engineer about the injured person; Next, wait for the coastguard to contact you. Do this correctly and the coastguard will be informed and may send a lifeboat or helicopter to assist with the evacuation. Just be careful: do not move the injured person unless there is immediate danger.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Show how to provide accurate information about number of persons on board, injuries, and safety equipment available.
gold_answer: On MRCC's request: "THIS IS (vessel), POB FIVE — TWO ADULTS UNINJURED, ONE ADULT UNCONSCIOUS FROM FALL, ONE ADULT WITH SUSPECTED FRACTURED WRIST, ONE CHILD AGED SEVEN UNINJURED. SAFETY EQUIPMENT: SIX PERSON LIFERAFT, FIVE LIFE JACKETS WORN, EPIRB ARMED, FLARES ON BOARD, OVER." Structured breakdown lets MRCC allocate appropriate medical and rescue resources.
expected_points: break down by age and injury
list safety equipment (liferaft, life jackets, EPIRB, flares)
answer: First, provide your position; Then, state the number of persons on board; Next, indicate if injured persons require medical assistance; After that, specify the type of assistance needed; Finally, confirm availability of lifeboats/liferafts; Then, report damage control status; Then, check for shortages of food/water; Then, inform about medical staff on board; Then, state if radio communication is possible; Then, indicate if engine(s) can be used; Then, confirm if the vessel can maneuver. Do this correctly and all relevant parties are informed of the vessel's condition and can respond appropriately. Just be careful: ensure all information provided is accurate to avoid miscommunication.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Perform a role-play reporting a grounding incident and requesting tide and salvage advice.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "PAN PAN x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), URGENCY: GROUNDED ON SANDBANK, VESSEL UPRIGHT, HULL INTACT, NO WATER INGRESS, POB FOUR ALL SAFE, REQUEST TIDAL INFORMATION AND SALVAGE ADVICE, OVER." MRCC will provide tidal predictions (next high water, predicted rise) and put you in touch with a local salvage/tug service. Log everything.
expected_points: PAN PAN x3, ALL STATIONS x3
request tidal info and salvage advice
answer: First, report your position; Then, report your present condition; Next, request tide information; After that, request salvage assistance. Do this correctly and the vessel's condition is assessed and appropriate assistance is requested. Just be careful: grounding can lead to significant damage and safety risks.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Demonstrate how to report a pollution incident (e.g., oil slick) using proper terminology.
gold_answer: On coastguard working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REPORTING POLLUTION INCIDENT, POSITION (…), OIL SLICK APPROXIMATELY TWO HUNDRED METRES BY FIFTY METRES, DARK BROWN COLOUR, HEAVY SHEEN, DRIFTING NORTH-EAST, NO SOURCE VESSEL VISIBLE, WIND (…), OVER." Coastguard tasks the appropriate marine pollution response and may issue a SÉCURITÉ warning. Provide any additional data (photos, samples, source vessel details).
expected_points: note any source vessel; coastguard tasks response
answer: First, report pollution; Then, specify the type of pollution; Next, indicate if the pollution is increasing or decreasing; After that, provide the exact position of the pollution; Finally, describe the visibility and weather conditions; Then, state the sea state; Then, mention any assistance required; Then, confirm the number of vessels in vicinity. Do this correctly and effective communication of pollution details to relevant authorities. Just be careful: ensure all information is accurate to avoid miscommunication.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Show how to respond to an MRCC request for continuous situation updates at defined intervals.
gold_answer: Acknowledge and set a mental or written schedule (e.g. every 15 minutes on the working channel). At each interval: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), UPDATE — POSITION (…), CONDITION (…), NO CHANGE / CHANGES: (…), NEXT UPDATE IN ONE FIVE MINUTES, OVER." If circumstances stabilise, ask MRCC to reduce the frequency. If they deteriorate, escalate immediately.
answer: First, commence continuous DSC watch on channel 70; Then, set your VHF radio to the working channel; Next, commence voice DSC watch on the working channel. Do this correctly and continuous monitoring of distress alerts and timely communication with the MRCC. Just be careful: ensure to monitor the correct channels as specified by the MRCC.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Perform a complete, realistic safety-related communication scenario integrating distress/urgency/safety decision-making, position reporting, and coordination with authorities.
gold_answer: Scenario: heavy weather, engine failure and crew injury combine progressively. Start with SÉCURITÉ warning for a hazard sighted, escalate to PAN PAN when engine fails and drift becomes serious, then PAN PAN MEDICO when crew is injured, and finally MAYDAY as vessel starts taking water. Each stage uses correct prefix, standard structure, SMCP phrases, and readback of MRCC instructions. Log every transition and reason. Debrief afterwards on decision-making, priority correctness and channel discipline.
expected_points: progressive escalation SÉCURITÉ → PAN PAN → PAN PAN MEDICO → MAYDAY
each stage uses correct prefix and structure
answer: First, acknowledge the incoming call from MV Blue Horizon; Then, confirm understanding of their situation; Next, request their current position; After that, acknowledge their position and express concern about their proximity to the channel; Finally, suggest they alter course to starboard; Then, inform them of the potential consequences if they do not comply; Then, monitor their status. Do this correctly and MV Blue Horizon was informed of the potential danger and advised to alter course. Just be careful: altering course is necessary to avoid collision.
